## [LLM Judges Fail Correlatedly, Undermining Stacked Agent Safety Gates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07359) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07359) empirically tests whether deterministic rule layers and LLM-based runtime gates for agent tool calls fail independently, using 1,119 labelled agent actions across three corpora. It finds that any two LLM judges compose to only about 1.2–1.4 multiplication-equivalent layers (n_mult), while a rule layer plus one judge composes to about 1.86–2.09 layers, showing that stacking LLM judges does not yield the multiplicative error reduction commonly assumed. This challenges a core assumption in AI agent safety design: that adding more independent gates multiplies reliability. If LLM judges share correlated errors, teams deploying stacked guardrails for tool-calling agents may be overestimating their real protection, which directly affects how safety mechanisms should be architected and evaluated. Under the STRICT miss definition, judge pairs show a median phi correlation of +0.430 (6 of 6 pairs significant) with floors of 1.02–1.17, while rule+judge pairs show a median phi of +0.014 (0 of 4 significant). Solo accuracy does not predict what a layer adds, and one judge tier was served by an unrequested model version in 50 of 112 batches, overturning a pre-declared analysis rule and reversing five conclusions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are increasingly given real tools—databases, shells, email, cloud APIs—and a single prompt injection or reasoning error can turn a benign agent into an exfiltration path. To mitigate this, practitioners stack runtime gates: deterministic rules plus LLM-as-judge filters that inspect each proposed tool call before execution. The common assumption is that independent gates multiply their error-reduction effects, much like independent layers in a reliability model, but this paper tests whether that assumption holds empirically.

## [Defense-in-Depth Framework Evaluates Memory Gates Against LLM Sycophancy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07403) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07403) introduces a 2×2 defense-in-depth framework that separates internal activation steering from external memory handling to combat memory-induced sycophancy in LLMs. It evaluates four open-weight models across 10 steering coefficients and five memory-defense configurations on a new benchmark called MemSyco-Bench, finding that selective Router Gate memory filtering preserves more accuracy than complete memory removal, while inverse steering's added benefit is not statistically significant. As LLMs increasingly use long-term memory to personalize interactions, retrieved user history can cause models to favor stored beliefs over objective evidence, a safety risk for AI alignment. This work provides a systematic evaluation framework and benchmark that helps the AI safety community understand which defenses actually work, showing that external memory filtering is more reliable than internal activation steering. The framework extracts sycophancy steering directions from 100 paired prompts and tests on MemSyco-Bench with 1,550 items (defense conditions judged on a 250-item subsample) using three LLM judges. On Llama 3.1 8B with Router Gate, mild inverse steering (α = -1.5) reduced judge-averaged sycophancy from 35.80% to 31.32% while accuracy moved from 43.99% to 43.31%, but this reduction was not statistically significant (paired p = 0.08 to 0.63 on 149 items).

## [Paper Proposes Formal Definition of Auditable Claims for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07459) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv position paper (2610.07459) proposes a formal definition of "auditable claims" for AI agents, requiring that a claim's policy, scope, records, and decision rule be fixed before any verdict is issued. It extends the Policy Checkability dimension of the authors' earlier Auditable Agents framework from single actions to claims, adding three agent-specific conditions: coverage by an independent record, authorization bound to each action's arguments, and completeness beyond integrity. The work directly targets a compliance gap in Article 12 of the EU AI Act, which mandates automatic event logging for high-risk systems but does not specify which records actually settle a given claim. By providing a conceptual foundation for AI governance and verification, it could influence how operators, buyers, auditors, and standard setters design and evaluate agent accountability mechanisms. The paper adapts the preconditions of an assurance engagement, defining a claim as auditable only when its elements and a decision rule are fixed in advance and the records are obtainable. Under an explicit model, the authors prove that support is impossible without each of the three agent-specific conditions wherever its hypotheses hold, and they apply the method to six common claims via a claim-check table anchored in current NIST, IETF, and OWASP drafts, followed by a worked case through five evidence states.

## [COMPASS: Steering Attention Heads to Elicit LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07469) ⭐️ 7.0/10

COMPASS is a new inference-time steering method that uses the correctness of a model's own direct answer attempts as a simple signal to identify a latent reasoning direction, then locates the small subset of attention heads where this direction can be effectively intervened using a logit-space attribution score. Across three model families and multiple math benchmarks, it improves GSM8K accuracy by 16 percentage points on average and approaches chain-of-thought accuracy while generating 20-70% fewer tokens. This work shows that eliciting reasoning may not require predefined characterizations of reasoning such as CoT prompt design or SAE-derived features, potentially simplifying how practitioners control and interpret LLM behavior. It also suggests reasoning capability is concentrated in remarkably few attention heads, which could inform future interpretability and model-editing research. The method requires only per-head activation statistics and its interventions transfer to unseen benchmarks without re-fitting; ablations confirm that both the correctness direction and the small set of heads carrying it are necessary, with the effect concentrated in remarkably few heads. However, the approach is demonstrated specifically for mathematical reasoning with verifiable answers, so its generalization to other reasoning domains remains to be tested.

Activation steering is an inference-time technique that modifies a model's internal activations to control its outputs, while sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular interpretability tool for extracting interpretable features from LLMs. COMPASS builds on these ideas but replaces the need for predefined reasoning features with a simple correctness signal.

## [Muon Optimizer Study Questions Need for Fine-Grained Spectral Shaping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07497) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper analyzes the spectral properties of the Muon optimizer and finds that approximately 94–97% of singular modes lie below an estimated noise edge, yet collectively align positively with the gradient. The authors propose BulkBoost, a two-band spectral reweighting framework that outperforms the fine-grained power-law profile of Freon and Spectra across 30 continued-pretraining settings from Pythia-14M to 410M. This work challenges the recent trend of designing increasingly fine-grained spectral shaping for Muon, suggesting that useful departures from the flat polar update are surprisingly low-dimensional. If validated, it could simplify future optimizer design and redirect research toward noise-calibrated, low-dimensional spectral interventions rather than per-mode gains. BulkBoost uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko–Pastur reference edge for Muon's Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from spikes above it, and applies one shared gain to increase the bulk's relative weight while preserving the Frobenius norm. Empirically, Freon reduces final loss by 0.022% of pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of 0.073–0.147%.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Muon is a recently proposed optimizer for 2D hidden-layer parameters that uses the polar update Q = UV^T from the matrix momentum M = UΣV^T, giving every singular direction equal weight (a flat profile). Recent optimizers like Freon and Spectra replace this flat profile with fine-grained spectral maps that assign each direction its own gain. The Marchenko–Pastur distribution from random matrix theory describes the asymptotic behavior of singular values of large random matrices and provides a statistical baseline for distinguishing signal from noise in the spectrum.

## [GroundAct Redefines Groundedness for Autonomous Driving Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07521) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces GroundAct, a framework that shifts the unit of grounding in autonomous driving from reasoning to physical entities and their interactions, creating an explicit path from what reasoning grounds to what the plan does, termed 'grounded planning'. It uses a lightweight reference token to keep each selected entity's continuous state addressable through symbolic reasoning, and only referenced entities' interactions with the evolving proposal correct the plan. This work addresses a fundamental gap in autonomous driving: correctly grounded reasoning does not guarantee desirable driving outcomes, as collisions can occur despite faithful reasoning. By redefining groundedness around physical entities and their interactions, GroundAct could improve generalization across diverse and long-tail scenarios, impacting the development of safer and more reliable autonomous driving systems. GroundAct is evaluated in both open-loop and closed-loop settings, showing strong open-loop planning across normal, out-of-distribution, and safety-critical scenarios, with closed-loop results extending evidence to driving in simulation. The framework is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.07521v1) and has not yet undergone peer review or community discussion.

**Background**: Autonomous driving models increasingly incorporate reasoning to support generalization across diverse and long-tail scenarios, grounding it in causal relationships, spatial structure, perceptual evidence, and predicted futures. ## [VALSE: Vertical Adaptive Layer Skipping for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07606) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VALSE introduces a theoretical framework for per-sample, non-contiguous layer skipping in large language models, proving three foundational results: an Expected FLOPs formula (theorem 2), function-space superset and strict inclusion theorems (theorems 10 and 11), and a structural duality between VALSE and Mixture-of-Experts architectures (proposition 6). Building on this theory, the paper proposes a lightweight difficulty estimator that scores each input from the first few layers and per-layer gates that selectively skip redundant layers, including arbitrary middle layers while retaining deeper ones. This work provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for adaptive layer skipping, a promising direction for reducing LLM inference cost, and its formal analysis of FLOPs and function-space properties could guide the design of more efficient and principled dynamic-depth models. The structural duality with Mixture-of-Experts positions vertical depth-wise sparsity as an orthogonal counterpart to horizontal width-wise sparsity, potentially opening new avenues for combining both forms of sparsity in future architectures. The paper establishes a closed-form Expected FLOPs formula for arbitrary per-sample skip schedules as a function of layer-wise skip probabilities, and proves that skip-layer models are strictly contained in—yet meaningfully approximate—the full-layer function space, with an explicit separating example. The feasibility of the proposed method is only preliminarily assessed at prototype scale, and it remains an arXiv preprint without community discussion yet.

However, symbolic-accuracy gains are less consistent across modules, random acquisition is competitive with disagreement scoring, and unequal batch constraints prevent attributing measurement savings solely to acquisition quality, leaving causal components and generalization beyond noiseless direct-equation tasks unresolved.

## [Injected-Truth Study Tests Whether Quant Admission Gates Really Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07701) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07701) introduces an injected-truth protocol with a random-admission control to test whether statistical admission gates in quantitative strategy research actually carry information or merely raise the bar for adoption. Across synthetic and real-calibrated panels, the gates eliminated false discoveries in weak-signal regimes but cut adoption to just 1–7%, added nothing when signals were strong, and silently rejected every candidate—including true signals—when criteria were computed on absolute rather than excess returns. This work offers a rigorous methodological caution for quantitative finance: admission gates can be effective at filtering false discoveries but may be so costly that they discard most genuine strategies, and the choice between absolute and excess return criteria can determine whether any strategy is ever adopted. It matters for researchers and practitioners who rely on statistical significance tests to decide which backtested strategies to deploy. The protocol's key innovation is a random-admission control that adopts strategies at the same rate as the gate, so a gate only proves informative if it beats this control; the study also shows that gates add no value in strong-signal regimes, meaning their benefit is concentrated in weak-signal settings where adoption collapses to 1–7%.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: In quantitative finance, researchers test many trading rules against the same historical data, so some strategies appear profitable purely by chance—a problem known as multiple testing or data snooping. Backtest overfitting occurs when a strategy is tuned to historical noise rather than a persistent market edge. Admission gates are statistical criteria (such as false discovery rate controls) that a strategy must pass before being adopted, but their real-world effectiveness and cost had not been rigorously tested. Excess returns measure performance relative to a benchmark, while absolute returns judge a strategy's raw return in isolation.

## [AgentMemGate Blocks Speculation Contamination in AI Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07707) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AgentMemGate introduces a write-time gate that classifies extracted statements as speculation, completed event, correction, or other, keeping unresolved plans out of the profile store until conditions promote or delete them. On a 147-conversation held-out set, the paper shows Mem0 and Graphiti assert unresolved plans as current state for 35.2% and 27.3% of pending plans, while AgentMemGate eliminates all observed contamination on the core benchmark and raises task accuracy from 65% to 95%. This work identifies a novel and important failure mode in long-term memory for LLM agents—speculation contamination—and shows that existing memory systems like Mem0 and Graphiti frequently make this error. As conversational assistants increasingly rely on persistent memory, preventing speculative statements from being stored as facts is critical for user trust and downstream task accuracy. The paper releases datasets, prompts, and evaluation code, and reports that on the harder held-out set gated contamination is 3.4% to 5.7% with task accuracy rising by 9 to 13 percentage points. The main remaining bottleneck is field matching: realistic speculations often match no profile field and never reach the gate.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Conversational AI assistants with long-term memory extract facts from user messages into a store that is consulted in later conversations, enabling personalization across sessions. A stated plan can enter that store as fact—for example, a user who might move to Seattle may be recorded as already living there—an error the authors call speculation contamination. Final-state memory benchmarks miss this error because they do not probe intermediate state and include few unresolved speculations. Write-time gating refers to selectively controlling modifications to a memory store at the point of ingestion, prior to retrieval or downstream use.

## [PERSIST Brings Cross-Session Who-What-When Memory to Full-Duplex Voice Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07725) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PERSIST is a new persistent memory system for multi-session, multi-speaker spoken dialogue that explicitly models Who, What, and When, structuring cross-session histories into readable event records retrieved via a 3W joint scoring mechanism combining semantic content, acoustic speaker identity, and temporal state. It reuses intermediate representations from the dialogue backbone to avoid query-audio re-encoding, cutting retrieval latency from 578.42 ms to 7.03 ms, and introduces SpokenTrace, a diagnostic benchmark on which it reaches 85.08% end-to-end task accuracy and lifts all-support EM@3 from 49.01% (BGE-large) to 82.10%. Shared voice assistants today typically cannot answer questions like "When did I originally plan to leave?" or distinguish one household member's past statements from another's, so PERSIST's joint modeling of speaker identity, content, and temporal state addresses a core limitation for personalized, context-aware assistants. The dramatic latency reduction also suggests persistent memory can be practical in real-time full-duplex interaction rather than only in offline retrieval settings. The system's 3W joint scoring combines semantic similarity with acoustic speaker identity and temporal state, and it explicitly distinguishes earlier plans from later revisions rather than just retrieving topically similar passages. Evaluation is factorized by memory task and speaker-query type on SpokenTrace, exposing failures in recall, speaker attribution, and temporal-state tracking; the work is an arXiv preprint and has not yet undergone peer review.

## [VisualNoiseQA: Benchmarking LLM Reasoning Under Noisy Visual Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07751) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07751) introduces VisualNoiseQA, a benchmark where a text-only LLM must solve VQA problems by iteratively querying a fixed, off-the-shelf VLM treated as a stochastic visual sensor. For each query, multiple samples are drawn and an empirical uncertainty signal is exposed via self-consistency, and the benchmark contains 1,000 instances spanning perception, chart understanding, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Most existing active reasoning benchmarks assume environmental feedback is trustworthy, so this work fills a gap by studying how LLMs should reason when the evidence itself is uncertain. It provides a controlled playground that could inform the design of more robust tool-using and sensor-querying agents in real-world settings. The benchmark construction is automatic and scalable: starting from diverse VQA sources and two noisy VLMs, only questions where the sensor is inconsistent yet human-solvable are retained. The uncertainty signal is derived from self-consistency across multiple samples rather than from an explicitly calibrated model, which is a notable design choice and limitation.

VisualNoiseQA combines these ideas by treating a vision-language model (VLM) as a noisy sensor whose answers vary across samples, and by giving the reasoner an uncertainty signal so it can decide what to ask next and when to stop.

## [ST-Bench: New Benchmark Tests Multi-Agent Systems on Scientific Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07763) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ST-Bench, a benchmark of 100 Earth science data analysis tasks (hydrology, agriculture, and wetland methane research) expanded into 2,067 expert-validated queries, to test whether LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) outperform single agents on real scientific data analysis. Evaluating five recent MAS generation methods under two training protocols against single-agent baselines on the same GPT-5 backbone, nine of ten MAS configurations beat the cheapest single-agent baseline, with the strongest reaching nearly three times its composite score. This addresses a key gap: MAS advantages have been demonstrated mainly on coding, math, and QA tasks where executable tests give a binary success signal, but it was untested whether that advantage transfers to real scientific data analysis. The finding that MAS specialization confers measurable but conditional benefit — driven mainly by coverage rather than metric quality — gives researchers and practitioners a clearer basis for deciding when multi-agent workflows are worth their extra inference cost. The gain is primarily attributable to coverage: trained workflows produce realistic numerical metrics on a larger fraction of queries, while the quality of those metrics, conditional on producing realistic output, is comparable to the single-agent baseline. The strongest configuration requires roughly four times the single-agent inference time, whereas a more economical workflow captures most of the benefit at less than twice the cost.

## [Quantization Effects on Tool-Failure Recovery Vary Across Prompts and Evaluation Designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07781) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07781) compares 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct across twenty deterministic tool-use tasks and five prompts, finding that the direction of the 8-bit vs 4-bit recovery comparison flips depending on the prompt, the evaluation target, and the scoring policy. For Llama under one prompt, scoring each variant only on its own clean-passing tasks favors 4-bit by 17.5 points, scoring the same tasks for both variants gives no difference, and scoring the full pipeline favors 8-bit by 28.3 points; applying strict output parsing then turns that +28.3 into -15.0. The finding warns practitioners that a single prompt, a single screened task set, or a single scoring policy cannot establish a stable conclusion about quantized-agent robustness, so deployment decisions based on such narrow evaluations may be misleading. It also implies that reported robustness gaps between 8-bit and 4-bit models should be treated as evaluation-design artifacts until matched-task, full-pipeline comparisons with stated scoring policies and quantified uncertainty are provided. On tasks both variants complete without faults under the same prompt, the 8-bit minus 4-bit recovery difference ranges from 0 to +20.2 percentage points for Llama and from -50.0 to +35.0 points for Qwen; full-pipeline point estimates favor 8-bit Llama under all five prompts, while the Qwen comparison changes direction across prompts. Executor leniency is a third design choice that can reverse results, and the authors recommend comparing variants on matched tasks, reporting full-pipeline success for deployment, stating the scoring policy, and quantifying uncertainty across tasks rather than injected fault sites.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses a trained language model's weights to lower bit-widths, such as 8-bit or 4-bit, to cut memory and compute costs without retraining. Language-model agents are systems that call external tools, and temporary tool failures are a common real-world condition they must recover from. This paper studies whether cheaper 4-bit quantization degrades that recovery ability relative to 8-bit, and shows the answer depends heavily on how the evaluation is set up.

## [Persistent Memory in Multi-Agent LLM Inference Adds Cost Without Accuracy Gain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07782) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A controlled study on arXiv (2610.07782) measured a three-tier agent architecture and found that decomposing long-context inference across cooperating agents cuts peak KV cache working set to 14.3 MiB per query versus 35.5 and 35.3 MiB for single-pass and retrieval-augmented baselines. However, adding a persistent memory tier that stores and recalls reasoning traces costs an extra +0.368 MiB of peak cache (95% CI [+0.167, +0.590]) while producing no detectable accuracy change (+0.015, 95% CI [-0.011, +0.046]) across eight controlled dataset pairs at n=100 per arm. This finding challenges a common assumption in multi-agent LLM system design that persistent memory tiers improve accuracy, suggesting that system designers may be paying memory overhead for no measurable benefit on single-question benchmarks. It also provides methodological guidance for how agent-memory ablations should be conducted and validated. The authors argue the null result is structural: single-question benchmarks supply each item with its own evidence and score it independently, and correctness requires resetting stored traces between conditions, so recall has nothing informative to retrieve. Reaching this conclusion required four measurement corrections — three that inflated the apparent benefit and a fourth that made an effect of that size look resolvable — none of which were visible in the results table.

**Background**: KV cache stores the key and value tensors from attention layers during LLM inference, and its memory footprint grows with sequence length and batch size, making it a key bottleneck for long-context workloads. Multi-agent architectures split long-context inference across cooperating agents to bound the active KV cache per call, and many such systems add a persistent memory tier that stores and recalls reasoning traces, typically validated by an ablation showing an accuracy gain. This paper tests both claims under controlled conditions with confidence intervals.

## [Attacca Trains Goal-Conditioned Policies for Long-Horizon Embodied Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07785) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Attacca is a new method that trains visual goal-conditioned policies on complete search-to-interact trajectories, using goal images decoupled from the execution environment. It introduces context-decoupled goal sampling, a target-mask prediction head for dense current-view grounding, and behavioral-phase conditioning for Search, Approach, and Interact stages, achieving 39.0-47.5% clean success in Minecraft and up to 7x improvement on long-horizon tasks. This addresses a critical gap in long-horizon embodied AI, where agents often fail to proceed when the next target is outside their field of view or the world state has changed. The approach could significantly improve the robustness of robots and embodied agents in continuous, multi-step tasks such as household service or navigation. Attacca pairs each demonstration with a class-compatible masked goal image from another world, removing direct scene and pose correspondence, and uses a target-mask prediction head for auxiliary supervision beyond action imitation. Evaluated in Minecraft, it achieves 54%, 30%, and 28% completion on long-horizon tasks, yielding up to a 7x improvement over baselines.

ThinkFuse is a training-free test-time fusion framework that compares segment-level uncertainty shifts against trajectory-level uncertainty trends to detect unstable reasoning points in small reasoning models (SRMs), then fuses auxiliary reasoning paths into the primary model's trajectory. Experiments show it outperforms baselines on mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks, with consistent gains across model-family combinations and robustness even when the primary model is smaller. Small reasoning models often fail to recover once their chain-of-thought enters an erroneous path, and existing test-time fusion methods that rely on local signals can be misled by transient uncertainty fluctuations. ThinkFuse's trajectory-aware selective triggering could make efficient small models more reliable for complex reasoning, reducing the need for costly large models. ThinkFuse is training-free and requires fewer fusion triggers while generating fewer tokens, highlighting the efficiency of selective triggering. The code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/ThinkFuse, though the work is currently an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [STEPGATE: Uncertainty-Aware Step-Level Handoff for Small Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07816) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces STEPGATE, an uncertainty-aware handoff framework that scores each action taken by a local small language model (SLM) and selectively escalates only the challenging steps to a stronger cloud model. On a 52-task held-out single-step BFCL-derived test split, the Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B pair reached 82.7% task success with 30.8% escalation, versus 67.3% for local-only and 75.4% for random escalation at a similar escalation rate. Most existing routers pick a model once per query, but agent tasks involve sequential decisions whose difficulty changes as intermediate observations arrive, so step-level escalation can recover much of the gap to a stronger backend while cutting remote inference and token transmission. This matters for teams deploying local SLM agents on edge devices or privacy-sensitive settings who want cloud-level reliability without paying cloud-level cost. In a separate multi-turn evaluation, STEPGATE achieved 69.0% trajectory success and 84.0% action success using only 30.0% cloud actions, compared with 48.0%/70.5% local-only, 60.0%/78.2% random escalation, and 57.0%/77.1% query-level routing, while a strong-only baseline reached 82.0% trajectory success at 100% cloud actions. The authors caution that evaluation is limited to one model family (Qwen2.5), a single stronger backend, scripted tasks, and small test sets, and that the risk tiers are research annotations rather than formal safety guarantees.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Small language models (SLMs) are attractive as local agent controllers because they reduce remote inference, latency, and deployment footprint, but they are more prone to structured tool-calling errors that can derail an agent step. Model routing is the practice of deciding which model handles a request, and the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) is a widely used benchmark for evaluating how accurately models call functions or tools. STEPGATE builds on these ideas by moving the routing decision from the query level down to the individual agent step.

## [DHCG Builds Dynamic Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM Multi-Agent Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07835) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07835) introduces DHCG, a framework that reframes LLM-based multi-agent system design as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) and dynamically determines both agent composition and scale during execution. It coordinates three modules — Planner, Worker, and Generator — to progressively build a hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch, and uses action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance, improving over a single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and beating static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77–8.02 points across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. Existing multi-agent systems suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, which restricts their ability to adapt to evolving reasoning requirements. By making agent composition and scale dynamic and training the Planner with preference optimization, DHCG offers a more adaptive orchestration paradigm that could improve reliability and efficiency for complex LLM-based reasoning tasks. This is a valuable technical contribution for AI/ML researchers working on multi-agent orchestration. DHCG models agent collaboration as a hierarchical directed acyclic graph where nodes denote agent executions and edges route outputs to define information dependencies. At each step, the Planner generates distinct, complementary roles tailored to current reasoning needs, selectively routes relevant information, and can either finalize the graph early or progressively expand it when more reasoning is required. The framework also generalizes across different Planner backbones and unseen Worker models.

**Background**: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) use multiple language-model agents that collaborate to solve complex problems, and recent research focuses on dynamically orchestrating these agents rather than using fixed pipelines. A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) is a mathematical framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, where the agent cannot directly observe the full underlying state and must act based on observations or belief states. DHCG applies this POMDP view to MAS design, treating the choice of which agents to create and how many as sequential decisions guided by execution feedback.

RA-MoWE introduces workflow-affinity embeddings that record how well a fixed set of reference workflows solves each query, then clusters queries by these embeddings to generate specialized, reusable expert workflows. On a 300-query test set spanning mathematics, science, and programming, it improves average task score by 4.04 percentage points over selecting among reference workflows while using 27.7% fewer language-model calls at inference. By clustering queries and reusing expert workflows, RA-MoWE points toward more efficient and scalable agentic systems that could reduce inference cost for production LLM agents. An embedding encoder predicts workflow-affinity embeddings directly from query text, so new queries can select a generated expert without first executing the reference workflows. Each cluster's queries and average embedding initialize and refine a specialized workflow through execution feedback; the approach is an arXiv preprint without community discussion or independent validation yet.

## [Self-Referenced Social Preferences Enable Cooperation Without Observing Others' Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07881) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07881) introduces self-referenced social preferences, a method where each agent learns a model of its own reward and applies it to other agents' observed transitions to assess their outcomes from its own perspective, without needing access to peers' private reward signals. Evaluated on three sequential social dilemmas—Escape Room, Clean Up, and Commons Harvest—the approach achieves cooperative behavior even where independent learners fail, and often produces more equitable divisions of jointly produced returns than agents with true rewards. This work removes a key assumption in multi-agent reinforcement learning—that agents can observe each other's rewards—which is often unrealistic in real-world settings where only behavior and outcomes are visible. It could enable more practical cooperative AI systems in domains like resource sharing, traffic, and public-good provision, and shows that explicit reward access is not necessary for learning cooperation. The paper studies two integration points: modifying the learning reward or weighting policy updates, and finds the best choice depends on the social preference—inequity aversion works best in the reward with a value look-ahead, while pure benevolence benefits from policy-update weighting. Under partial observability, the policy-update approach continues to support cooperation.

## [Isotropic Yet Undecodable: Sequential Content-Sufficiency Gap in Latent-Predictive Text Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07906) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07906) introduces an information-theoretic decomposition that separates input ambiguity, representation loss, and readout mismatch, and shows that perfect agreement and joint isotropic Gaussianity can coexist with zero target information. To address this, the authors propose CANOPE, a nonautoregressive framework with ordered latent canvases, canonical-token supervision, and geometric regularization, which achieves 98.8% positional Recall@1 for token-grounded (PL2) representations versus 13.5% for latent-agreement (PL0) under strong natural corruption. This work challenges the common assumption that geometrically regular latent representations are sufficient for downstream tasks, showing that isotropic Gaussian structure alone does not guarantee recoverable sequential content. It has implications for representation learning, nonautoregressive text generation, and any pipeline that relies on latent encodings for ordered prediction, potentially reshaping how researchers evaluate and design text representations. On 40,000 validation sequences, PL0 and PL2 have nearly identical pooled ranks but drastically different positional Recall@1 (13.5% vs. 98.8%) when the correct target length is provided; on 3,930 LJSpeech validation utterances, frozen PL2 with a trained MatchaTTS readout yields 21.54% WER on corrupted text versus 99.22% for frozen PL0, while end-to-end MatchaTTS reaches 10.93% WER. The paper also shows that token log-loss provides a one-sided information-loss bound and that rank alone cannot determine prediction risk.

The paper introduces the Continuous Memory Machine (CMM), a recurrent architecture with separate matrix-valued short-term and long-term memory states that are jointly updated by a Transformer. Built on the Continuous Thought Machine (CTM), the CMM outperforms a broad suite of baselines on algorithmic, in-context learning, and recurrent reasoning tasks while preserving interpretable attention patterns, with code released at github.com/SakanaAI/continuous-memory-machines. Standard RNNs compress all information into a single vector-valued state, forcing short-term computation and long-term retention to share one representation, which limits sequence modeling. By separating these roles and adding an expressive bidirectional read-write mechanism, the CMM could advance memory-augmented neural networks and long-context reasoning, benefiting researchers working on sequence modeling and memory architectures. The CMM's short-term memory tracks recent neural activity, with uniquely parameterized neuron-level models learning to use these activity patterns for computation, while a persistent long-term memory stores information for later use. A Transformer jointly updates both stores, allowing each to reorganize its own contents and both read from and write to the other, though the work remains an arXiv preprint and its practical scalability is not yet fully established.

## [SpeedrunBench Tests LLM Agents on Video Game Speedrunning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08076) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SpeedrunBench, a new benchmark that evaluates frontier LLM agents across 9 video games by having them attempt speedrunning tasks. Agents must repeatedly refine strategies, reflect on performance, and reason over long action horizons to beat both their own and others' completion times. This benchmark addresses the timely question of whether LLM agents can go beyond human-developed solutions, a capability that becomes critical as well-trodden solutions prove insufficient for problems lacking context or training data. It offers a saturation-resistant evaluation measure, since there is almost always a faster completion time waiting to be discovered. Experiments show frontier agents approach human world records in simple platformer games but remain behind human performance on longer, more complex games under practical budgets. The benchmark covers 10+ frontier agents and evaluates them in three settings: an online computer-use setting and two new offline settings.

## [Self-Retrospection Distillation Turns Hindsight into Foresight for RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08077) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08077) introduces Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD), which uses post-hoc trajectory experience to supervise pre-interaction foresight predictions, addressing the vanishing reward signal in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) under group-relative objectives. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains up to 24.2 percentage points, and in a 2B setting where 98% of rollout groups are all-failure, RLVR alone reaches 0.0% success while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget. This work tackles a core limitation of group-relative RL methods like GRPO, where uniform rewards within a rollout group produce zero learning signal, a problem that becomes severe as models scale and tasks get harder. By showing that post-hoc experience can shape predictive representations before interaction, SRD could influence future RLVR research and improve sample efficiency for agentic and reasoning tasks. SRD distills privileged hindsight from a completed trajectory into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy, and this foresight serves only as a training target that need not be generated at inference time. The advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce, with 37–98% of rollout groups being reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD still extracts learning signal from sampled trajectories.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) trains models using automatically checkable outcome rewards, and it has become popular for improving long chain-of-thought reasoning. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), used by DeepSeek-R1, samples a group of answers per prompt and uses the group's average reward as a baseline, but when all rollouts in a group receive the same reward, the relative advantage becomes zero and no gradient signal is produced. SRD proposes prospective learning, in which hindsight from completed trajectories supervises foresight predictions made from the pre-interaction view.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08101) defines "execution consistency" in multi-agent systems through duties governing state use, information handoffs, and final-state agreement, showing that identical retained memory records can correspond to both compliant and violating executions under the same task rule. Controlled removal of evidence such as receipt, action dependence, or response validity leaves 82.4% of opposite-label pairs indistinguishable, while restoration separates 97.9% of merged pairs; the authors' CAVERT framework outperforms contract-prompted LLM and rule-based baselines across all 12 benchmark-executor settings. This work exposes a critical gap in current memory governance and failure diagnosis approaches, which regulate or inspect recorded information but cannot by themselves establish whether agents actually fulfilled their task duties. It has direct implications for AI safety and multi-agent coordination, suggesting that agent-memory and execution interfaces must preserve specific execution evidence for reliable compliance judgment. The core claim is that identical retained records can correspond to compliant and violating executions under the same task rule, and natural-log annotations identify the defined violations in actual executions. However, existing logs do not always explicitly represent the execution relationships needed for these judgments, which is why the CAVERT framework is used to extract supported relationships from logs; it also outperforms rule-guided recovery in all four evaluated environments under the same gate and executor limits.

## [ML infers alloy composition and process parameters from microstructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08165) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08165) investigates whether the inverse step of alloy development — going from an optimized microstructure and texture back to the alloy composition and processing parameters — can be learned. Using an in-house dataset of 107 magnesium alloy extrusion conditions across 14 alloys, the authors compare three microstructure descriptors (conventional grain/texture statistics, a pretrained vision embedding, and a graph neural network on the grain network) paired with prediction heads for two tasks: inferring composition given the process, and inferring process parameters given the composition. Alloy development traditionally runs forward, tuning structure until a target property is met, while the backward step from optimized structure to recipe still relies on expert knowledge. Demonstrating that this inverse mapping can be partially learned could accelerate alloy design and reduce reliance on costly trial-and-error experiments in materials informatics. Under 5-fold cross-validation, conventional descriptors identified the correct alloy for 65% of held-out conditions versus 17% for always guessing the most common alloy, while the learned embeddings stayed below 30%. Process parameters were recoverable but noisier — microstructure roughly halved the temperature error compared with using composition alone — and because only a few alloys and press settings were used, heads that pick from known discrete options while respecting their order outperformed free-value regression.

## [QEMFN uses trainable quantum entanglement for vision-language fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08216) ⭐️ 7.0/10

QEMFN introduces a hybrid quantum-classical framework that uses parameterized entanglement circuits as an inductive bias for fusing image and text embeddings, outperforming classical baselines such as MLP, tensor fusion, FiLM, cross-attention, and compact transformers on COCO-5k and Flickr30k under matched parameter budgets and identical frozen CLIP backbones. The work includes an ablation suite, quantum-centric analyses of entangling capability, expressibility, and gradient variance, and execution on shot-based estimation, a noise-modeled fake backend, and a real superconducting device with zero-noise extrapolation. This work positions trainable entanglement as an interpretable, hardware-executable fusion mechanism at scales accessible on contemporary quantum devices, offering a new direction for multimodal retrieval research. It also provides a controlled empirical and quantum-centric evaluation that could guide future hybrid quantum-classical system design, even though it does not claim quantum computational advantage. QEMFN projects pretrained visual and textual features into compact latent spaces, encodes them as angle-parameterized quantum states, processes them through intra-modal and paired cross-modal entangling circuits, and measures the outputs for retrieval. The paper explicitly does not claim quantum computational advantage; its contribution is the framework and evaluation, with quantum-centric analyses including Meyer-Wallach entangling capability, expressibility, gradient variance against barren-plateau bounds, and entropy-performance correlation.

## [Contextual Priors Can Reverse Confidence-Correctness Ordering in Neural Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08229) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08229) shows that contextual priors used in neural-to-language decoding can reverse the relationship between confidence and correctness, so that some errors become more confident without any change in accuracy. Using MEG-MASC and MOUS datasets with local decoding scores, additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence, the authors find that pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87, but AUROC separating repairs from residual errors drops from 0.70 at initial ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50. This finding challenges the common assumption that higher confidence always indicates higher correctness, which is critical for brain-computer interfaces and neural-to-language decoding where confidence estimates are used for selective prediction. It implies that confidence after contextual fusion should retain local and contextual evidence separately, not just the fused scores, and the authors show that reading them separately improves selective decoding from 56.7% to 74.5% coverage while 92% of output sets still contain the correct candidate. The reversal is explained by a score-level account: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, limiting its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. A causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted, and under a word-level LM prior it keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence.

## [zkLLMPoT Certifies LLM Checkpoints Without Proving Full Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08258) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced zkLLMPoT, a zero-knowledge framework that certifies auditor-defined properties of a trained LLM checkpoint through forward evaluation rather than verifying the full optimization trajectory. It uses a two-phase protocol where the trainer first commits the architecture and weights, then the auditor selects challenge sequences, and the trainer proves the objective value on those sequences, making certification cost independent of training iterations. This addresses a major obstacle in auditing private LLM training, where model weights and training data cannot be revealed and cryptographically proving the entire training process is prohibitively expensive at Transformer scale. It could enable more trustworthy verification of model claims in privacy-preserving machine learning and regulated AI deployments. The framework builds on sumcheck- and lookup-based arguments to certify Transformer computations and supports next-token loss and task-specific audit objectives. The method is replay-free, meaning it does not store or revisit old task data, and it combines adaptive null space projection with semantic routing to balance knowledge accumulation against task-specific adaptation. ## [Standardization Trap Distorts Analysis of Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08314) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08314) identifies a 'standardization trap' in testing whether pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) use fixed-weight prediction for in-context learning, because public TFM packages standardize labels before the model sees them, causing ordinary derivatives to falsely suggest nonlinearity. The authors propose two certificates based only on predictions at standardized labels, and across five public TFMs they find evidence of 'joint processing,' where changing one context label alters how other labels influence the prediction. This work matters because it challenges a common assumption that in-context learning in tabular foundation models can be explained by simple fixed-weight schemes like linear regression or kernel smoothing. It provides a rigorous methodological tool for interpretability research and could influence how future TFM explanations are designed and validated. The two certificates can reject fixed-weight prediction and sums of independent nonlinear label transformations, and the authors find that joint processing emerges with training and that attention scores carry most of the measured interaction. The analysis is limited to five public TFMs and relies on prediction-level certificates rather than full mechanistic understanding.

## [AnyBottle Builds Compact Task-Specific Concept Bottleneck Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08552) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose AnyBottle, a single recipe for building compact, task-specific concept bottleneck models (CBMs) that dynamically selects concepts from an unsupervised pool (such as a sparse autoencoder) using a black-box teacher trained on the same frozen backbone. Each selection round adds the concept that best explains the bottleneck's current failures, with candidates restricted to regions of teacher/student disagreement, and nested dropout over the selection order lets the final bottleneck predict accurately from any concept prefix. This addresses a key limitation of annotation-free CBMs, which typically rely on large, static concept vocabularies that produce bottlenecks larger than any task needs and are harder to inspect. By showing that a small, discovered vocabulary can be as expressive as a much larger fixed one, AnyBottle could enable more interpretable and efficient models across vision and text domains. The method assumes only a frozen backbone and an unsupervised concept pool, and since no stage is modality-specific, adapting to a new domain or task requires swapping only the backbone and concept pool. Across six vision and two text datasets and two teacher paradigms, AnyBottle yields bottlenecks with fewer concepts and higher concept consistency than annotation-free baselines while staying close to the black-box reference.

## [PPWM: Parallel Predictive World Models for Long-Horizon Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08627) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Parallel Predictive World Models (PPWM), which predict a finite-horizon trajectory in parallel while retaining causal interaction among future representations, rather than feeding predicted states back autoregressively. Across four visual-control tasks, PPWM achieved the lowest long-horizon prediction error, the highest Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) simulator success, and more than a 3× average CEM planning speedup over the autoregressive LeWM baseline. This work suggests that accurate and efficient long-horizon world-model planning does not require state-by-state autoregression, which could substantially reduce planning latency in model-based reinforcement learning. If the approach generalizes, it may benefit robotics and visual control systems where fast, reliable multi-step planning is critical. PPWM conditions each horizon on its causal action prefix and lets future representations interact before decoding, separating temporal causality from state-by-state output recursion. The paper formalizes autoregressive rollout as a causal trajectory map and identifies the decoded-state feedback pathway that PPWM removes, though results are limited to four visual-control tasks and comparison against the LeWM baseline.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: World models are learned simulators that predict future states of an environment, and they are commonly used in model-based reinforcement learning to plan actions without interacting with the real environment. Traditional long-horizon planning relies on autoregressive rollouts, where each predicted state is fed back into the model to generate the next one, creating a long sequential computation path and exposing later predictions to accumulated decoding errors. The Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) is a popular sampling-based planner in model-based reinforcement learning that iteratively updates an action distribution using the top-performing sampled trajectories.

## [SquidAgent Cuts Hidden Costs of Parallel LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08647) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08647) identifies two hidden costs—re-exploration and alignment—that make parallel LLM multi-agent systems slower than serial baselines, and proposes a token-based decision criterion for when to parallelize a layer. The resulting system, SquidAgent, forks workers directly from the orchestrator's session and uses a pre-generated shared convention block, achieving a 2.2× mean throughput improvement and 2.6× mean wall-time speedup over Claude Code. This work challenges the common assumption that parallelizing LLM agents yields near-linear speedups, offering a principled criterion that could reshape how multi-agent systems are designed and scheduled. If validated, it could help developers avoid wasteful parallelism and improve latency and throughput in production agent pipelines. Because LLMs are poorly calibrated at estimating wall-clock time, SquidAgent measures cost in predicted output tokens instead, which the authors find LLMs estimate more reliably. A deterministic scheduler then applies the criterion layer by layer, and the approach also achieves a 2.0× throughput improvement over the strongest multi-agent baseline.

## [ParanoiaEval benchmarks unnecessary defensive work in coding agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08662) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents, grounded in the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance (ATMA) framework from software engineering risk management. It contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence, plus dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness evaluated by a human-calibrated agentic judge. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models found unnecessary risk treatment in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, and stronger task capability did not guarantee more appropriate risk treatment, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension that affects developer experience. This could reshape how autonomous coding agents are assessed and improved, since over-defensive behavior wastes effort and harms usability even when tasks are completed. The benchmark operationalizes the four ATMA treatments for coding-agent settings and uses a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation; experiments also revealed systematic patterns consistent with established human risk-management findings, suggesting human practice knowledge can guide diagnosis and improvement. As an arXiv preprint with a truncated abstract, the experimental depth and community validation remain limited.

## [Full-Duplex Speech Models Show Delayed Turn-Taking in Self-Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08683) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08683) paired two PersonaPlex-7B instances on a shared clock for unscripted conversation and measured their floor-transfer timing, finding a median of 400-560 ms versus 137 ms for humans in the Switchboard corpus. The timing was coupled between the two models, but delaying one direction of the channel shifted responses one-for-one, indicating a reactive wait after the perceived turn end rather than human-like turn-end projection. As full-duplex speech models are increasingly used in self-play data generation, agent societies, and model-based evaluation, their turn-taking timing directly shapes the quality of generated dialogue and multi-agent interactions. The 3-4x timing gap and reactive rather than predictive mechanism suggest current models may produce unnatural conversational rhythms when talking to each other, which could propagate into downstream training data and evaluation benchmarks. The study found that re-pairing speakers across conversations destroys the coupled timing, and that the last 120 ms of a partner's turn—where human projection places about a tenth of its transfers—holds only 1% of the models' transfers. The authors interpret this as consistent with a reactive wait mechanism rather than the predictive turn-end projection that characterizes human timing.

## [BOTTLED Benchmark Tests Whether LLM Agents Can Bottle Capabilities Cheaply](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08775) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces BOTTLED, a benchmark that gives LLM agents an entire unlabelled workload and requires them to complete it under fixed time, compute, and LLM API budgets, choosing their own approach such as training a small model or writing a reusable program. Across ten models and three tasks, the authors find that strong zero-shot performance does not reliably translate into strong bottling ability, with 48 of 60 bottling runs scoring below the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval of their model's zero-shot performance. This work matters because it reframes agent evaluation around amortised cost and reusable artifacts rather than one-off task accuracy, which is critical as organizations look to deploy LLM agents on large, repetitive workloads. It suggests that current agent benchmarks may overstate practical usefulness, and it provides a foundation for improving resource-aware agent deployment. Bottling can still yield substantial savings: on query-product relevance classification, Opus 5 retains about 82% of its zero-shot macro-F1 at roughly 657 times lower reported cost, and recovers about 94% of Jev's macro-F1 at a quarter of Jev's projected full-workload cost. However, 31 of 60 runs underperform the stronger of two small-model distillation baselines with the same token budget, and the benchmark is a preprint without community discussion yet.

## [RV-PI Learns When to Refine Budgeted Neural-Operator PDE Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06883) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formulates budgeted adaptive neural-operator solving for time-dependent PDEs, where a global Fourier neural operator advances the full field, a local operator proposes patch-wise residual corrections, and a set-aware selector chooses where to refine. It introduces rollout-verified policy improvement (RV-PI), which evaluates feasible refinement counts through actual continuation rollouts and accepts an update only when held-out trajectory error improves. This work shows that under a fixed refinement budget, the value of a local correction depends on its downstream effect on the autoregressive trajectory, not only on its immediate error reduction. It could improve the reliability and efficiency of neural-operator surrogates for scientific computing, benefiting researchers working on PDE simulation and scientific machine learning. On the shallow-water benchmark with a 32-intervention budget, RV-PI achieves a three-seed mean trajectory relative L2 error of 0.6910, improving over immediate-only policy improvement by 5.37% and RandomMacro by 2.41%. On the forcing-driven Brusselator benchmark with a 76-intervention budget, RV-PI attains 0.09954, improving over immediate-only policy improvement by 2.31% and RandomMacro by 5.32%.

## [Low-rank equilibrium computation for APT vs. moving target defense games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06885) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proves that the attack and defense influence matrices in industrial control system (ICS) dynamics are intrinsically low-rank, and that this structure propagates through the non-smooth Bellman operator of the zero-sum stochastic game. The authors propose DLR-NE (dynamical low-rank equilibrium computation), which augments the rank-r search space each iteration, regularizes the core matrix spectrum, and retracts via truncated SVD, achieving a Theta(n/r^2) speedup over full-rank value iteration with certified robustness. Equilibrium computation for stochastic security games has been prohibitively expensive at industrial state dimensions, limiting the practical deployment of game-theoretic moving target defense. By exploiting low-rank structure, this work makes certified, robust defense strategies computationally feasible for real ICS deployments, potentially affecting how critical infrastructure is protected against advanced persistent threats. The method provides four guarantees: an explicit approximation error bound, geometric convergence to a neighborhood with five physically interpretable error sources, per-step cost of O(nr^2), and a robustness knob where a single weight trades accuracy against certified safety. Experiments on a nonlinear power-system testbed confirm 94% parameter compression at only 0.16% utility loss, though the approach assumes the low-rank structure holds and requires tuning the rank parameter r.

**Background**: Moving target defense (MTD) is a proactive cyber defense strategy that constantly reconfigures system components to make attacks harder, while advanced persistent threats (APTs) are stealthy, prolonged attacks that infiltrate through a few entry points. Stochastic games model the interaction between an attacker and defender as a zero-sum game, and solving for a Nash equilibrium typically requires value iteration over the Bellman operator, which becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of system states grows. Low-rank approximation reduces high-dimensional matrices to a lower-rank form, and this paper shows that the influence matrices in ICS dynamics naturally exhibit such structure.

The analysis covers four open-weight models and reports retention ranges rather than a single number, with code and raw results released for reproducibility.

## [AttSVD: Prompt-Adaptive Low-Rank KV Cache Compression via Attention-Guided SVD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06927) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AttSVD introduces a training-free, prompt-adaptive low-rank compression for the KV cache that derives a truncated SVD basis from each prompt's own attention geometry, keeping every token instead of evicting them. It offers accumulating and streaming decode-time caching strategies plus two refinements—a per-matrix energy rule and an attention-aware basis truncation—and matches dense-cache performance on an agentic benchmark and the full LongBench suite while using up to 50% of the KV-cache memory. KV cache memory grows linearly with context length and dominates memory use in long-context inference, so a training-free compression that preserves all tokens could substantially lower serving costs for long-context and agentic LLM workloads. Because it avoids irreversible token eviction, it may also be more robust than eviction-based methods on tasks that depend on distant context. The compression operates along the feature axis rather than the sequence axis, cutting persistent per-head KV memory in proportion to the retained rank, and the same SVD factors provide free per-head interpretability into effective rank and the geometry attention consumes. The method is training-free and evaluated across multiple models, though the abstract does not specify which models or the exact rank/energy thresholds used.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: In autoregressive transformers, the KV cache stores key and value vectors for all previously processed tokens so that generation does not recompute them, but its size grows linearly with context length. Low-rank approximation via singular value decomposition (SVD) replaces a matrix with a lower-rank one that captures its dominant directions, and attention mechanisms determine which token representations a model actually reads. AttSVD combines these ideas by using each prompt's attention geometry to decide which directions to keep in the compressed KV cache.

## [Low-Rank Decision Operator Cuts Skill Injection Cost 100x](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06950) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper introduces a System-1 decision operator trained by behavior cloning that uses only 330K parameters to match a 1.33M-parameter reinforcement-learning-trained operator, while collapsing 3,685-token deliberation into a 6-token decision with no accuracy loss. A rank-4 variant with just 23K parameters (1/58 of the strongest published skill operator) suffices for SearchQA and nearly suffices for LiveMath, and the recipe transfers across five tasks and three backbones. This work shows that injecting skills into frozen language models can be dramatically cheaper and faster than current reinforcement-learning pipelines, potentially making skill adaptation accessible without large-scale training infrastructure. The finding that skills compose as approximately linear operators that can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped at inference time could enable modular, on-the-fly model customization. The performance gap to prior work is attributed to trainability set jointly by initialization and architecture: prior operators' initialization zeroes the gradient of both large factor matrices at the first optimization step, whereas this method's zero-initialized output projection inside a shared low-rank backbone receives a gradient immediately, confirmed by a gradient-flow probe. The gain is not chain-of-thought compression—23 of 57 LiveMath points beat the base model's best-of-8 sampling, and a logit-lens probe shows the operator amplifies the answer along the model's existing late-layer pathway rather than writing it earlier.

**Background**: Behavior cloning is the simplest form of imitation learning, using supervised learning to train a policy that mimics expert action distributions from demonstrations. The System-1 versus System-2 distinction from cognitive science describes fast, automatic, intuitive decisions versus slow, deliberate reasoning, and this paper frames its operator as a System-1 decision module.

## [APEX defends LLM agents at the execution boundary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06966) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.06966) introduces APEX, an active defense for LLM agents that enforces authorization and information endorsement at the execution boundary rather than trying to recognize attack patterns. It compiles a single authorization contract before untrusted execution, combining evidence-gated prevention with deception-based exposure, and reports 0% attack success on five of six benchmarks and 0.56% on the sixth against 13 baselines. Indirect prompt injection is one of the most pressing security problems for agents that read untrusted web content, tool outputs, or MCP server responses, and pattern-based defenses keep falling behind new injection carriers. By tying protection to what the trusted task permits rather than to how an attack is built, APEX could offer a more stable and general defense that applies uniformly across Tools, MCP servers, and Skills. The defense rests on two conditions settled by the trusted task: whether a proposed effect is authorized, and whether the runtime information reaching it is endorsed by that task. Evidence-gated prevention admits an effect only when the contract justifies it, while deception-based exposure makes unendorsed use reveal itself before the effect commits; the authors report 0% attack success under adaptive attacks on all three capability-unit types and effectiveness across different defender backbones, with code released on GitHub.

## [CrystalJev reframes atomistic foundation models as fast probabilistic decision-makers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06985) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CrystalJev introduces a framework that queries a frozen interatomic potential once per unrelaxed structure and answers typed questions with calibrated probabilities, finite-sample guarantees, and a rule for when to invoke slower relaxation. Across 65 Matbench Discovery models, a single forward pass decides nearly as well as a full relaxation at a thirtieth of the cost, and a value-of-information theory routes slower computation only where decisions can change. It also provides a principled statistical layer that the broader AI-for-science community can apply to other atomistic foundation models. The method achieves near-relaxation accuracy with a single forward pass, and in a registered prospective test with 700 new density-functional calculations, single-pass forecasts calibrated only on existing data over-stated the stable fraction of unseen candidates (5.8%) by at most 2.1 percentage points. The same layer generalizes to electronic, mechanical, and molecular questions.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.06994) introduces TARE, a method that runs a defense on a never-poisoned twin of the same recipe, schedule, and seed to measure the 'tare' — the clean-accuracy loss caused by the defense itself rather than by backdoor removal. The paper shows that in BackdoorBench, three attacks (WaNet, BPP, Input-Aware) ship a MultiStepLR scheduler that never fires, so their victims never anneal and are the least accurate in 30 of 31 public CIFAR cells at ≤5%, causing fine-tuning defenses to report negative removal costs that the benchmark clips to zero. A 2×2 editing of only the scheduler line isolates the cause: the sign of the fine-tuning family's clean-model cost reverses both ways while its published gain on the annealed victim only shrinks toward zero, replicated across 44/44 seeds, BPP, FT-SAM, CIFAR-100, VGG19-BN, and a second toolkit. On the BadNets grid, seven of eight defenses charge the twin (Neural Cleanse only where its detector fires), from +0.13 (fine-tuning) to +5.70 points (I-BAU), while ABL destroys it; the paper ships a three-key patch, a signed tare column (7 attacks × 8 defenses), and TARE-Z, a twin-free estimator for seed-stable defenses.

## [MaskAhead: Training-Free KV Cache Eviction for Block Diffusion LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06996) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MaskAhead introduces a training-free, mask-query-based ranking mechanism that handles both KV selection and eviction in block diffusion language models, using current-block masks for selection and probes of upcoming masked blocks for eviction. Its quantized variant Q-MaskAhead computes selection and attention directly from low-bit KV, and on long-prompt QA it reduces KV memory by up to 20.1x with only a 2.3-point mean F1 loss. Block diffusion language models keep a large KV cache across all denoising steps, which limits both memory capacity and generation speed, so a training-free way to shrink that cache could make such models far more practical to deploy. The reported 1.23x end-to-end and 1.68x decode-stage speedups in a batch-32 profile suggest real systems-level gains for efficient LLM inference. Experiments cover Fast-dLLM-v2, DreamReasoner, and LLaDA2.0-mini across long-generation reasoning, long-prompt question answering, and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval; on long-prompt QA, MaskAhead cuts KV memory by 9.5x on average with a 1.2-point mean F1 loss versus dense inference. The trade-off is that the more aggressive Q-MaskAhead variant raises memory reduction to 20.1x but increases the mean F1 loss to 2.3 points.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Block diffusion language models interpolate between autoregressive and discrete denoising diffusion paradigms, generating text in blocks that are refined over multiple denoising steps. Because each denoising step attends to the entire key-value cache of past tokens, the cache grows large and becomes a bottleneck for memory and speed. KV cache eviction addresses this by retaining only a fixed-size subset of key-value pairs and discarding the rest, but deciding which entries to keep is nontrivial.

**Background**: ReRAM (resistive random-access memory) is a non-volatile memory technology that stores data by changing resistance across a dielectric material, offering high density and near-zero leakage. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) places computation directly inside memory arrays, which is attractive for the memory-intensive matrix-vector multiplications of deep neural networks. However, fabrication process variations and defects make ReRAM devices error-prone, and faults such as stuck-at-high or stuck-at-low can corrupt the analog computation and degrade CNN accuracy.

Tool calling latency is a major bottleneck for LLM agents that must emit multiple calls or many argument fields per response, so a 4x throughput gain could make agentic systems noticeably more responsive and cheaper to run. **Background**: Speculative decoding is an inference-time optimization for autoregressive LLMs that generates multiple tokens per decoding step by having a smaller draft model propose tokens and the target model verify them, preserving output quality. ## [SPEAR: Five Principles for Interactive Human-Agent Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07204) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv position paper (arXiv:2610.07204) proposes SPEAR, a framework of five pillars for interactive human-agent alignment: Specification, Process, Evaluation, Adaptation, and Recalibration. It argues that alignment should be treated as an ongoing interaction design problem rather than a one-time pre-deployment optimization. The paper challenges the dominant paradigm of collecting human feedback, learning preferences, and finetuning models before deployment, which under-specifies how agents should behave in situated, long-term, and social contexts. Its reframing could influence both AI alignment research and human-agent interaction design practices as agentic systems become more autonomous. The five SPEAR pillars cover how people express intent and build shared understanding (Specification), how agents decide when to act, ask, defer, or pause (Process), how people judge agent success (Evaluation), how agents adapt to users over repeated use (Adaptation), and how people adjust trust, expectations, and behavior in response to agents (Recalibration). As a position paper, it offers a conceptual framework rather than empirical results or a technical system.

**Background**: AI alignment generally refers to steering AI systems toward a person's or group's intended goals, preferences, or ethical principles, and much recent work treats it as a pre-deployment optimization problem solved by feedback collection and finetuning. Human-agent interaction (HAI) is a related field focused on how users interact with non-deterministic agentic systems, and researchers have begun proposing design principles and evaluation heuristics for such interactions. Situated agents, which select actions based on locally perceived state rather than long-term planning, further complicate alignment because their behavior unfolds over time in social contexts.

## [DRMoET: Distributionally Robust Training for Mixture-of-Experts Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07207) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Distributionally Robust MoE Training (DRMoET), a drop-in objective that treats layer-wise experts as endogenous robustness groups and optimizes high-loss routing outcomes instead of merely equalizing traffic. Under the FLAME-MoE recipe at 10.3B total parameters and 67B training tokens, DRMoET improves the seven-task average from 0.6625 to 0.6767, while the auxiliary-loss-free baseline reaches 0.6431. This work addresses a hidden reliability problem in sparse MoE models: imperfect routing can send tokens to experts that are insufficiently trained for the assigned inputs, even when load balancing looks healthy. By showing that routing robustness—not just utilization balance—improves downstream performance at scale, it offers a practical objective for reliable sparse MoE scaling that could affect how large language models are trained. DRMoET updates a per-layer expert distribution using an entropy-regularized softmax rule on EMA-smoothed, activation-weighted expert losses, strengthening plausible non-top routing paths while preserving standard MoE computation. Mechanistic analyses show lower expert-loss variance with nearly unchanged mean loss, 4.3% lower excess loss under forced mid-k misrouting, and improved domain-expert specialization.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformers scale model capacity by activating only a few experts per token, replacing dense feed-forward layers with multiple expert sub-networks and a router that selects among them. This sparsity keeps computation low but creates a reliability risk: if routing is imperfect, tokens may be sent to experts that were not sufficiently trained on similar inputs. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) is a framework for decision-making under uncertainty where the data distribution itself is uncertain, and DRMoET adapts this idea to the MoE routing problem.
