## [TIDE 2.0: Open Model-Agnostic Engine for Keyed Clinical Note De-identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07224) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers from Stanford Medicine released TIDE 2.0, an MIT-licensed, model-agnostic engine that separates clinical note de-identification into an interchangeable recognizer and a keyed anonymizer, both running on institution-owned hardware. They also released TIDE2-Sentry, a recognizer distilled from a large language model, which achieved span-level recall of 0.88 in-domain and 0.77 on a second institution's corpus at precision 0.88 and 0.87. Clinical notes cannot be used for research until protected health information is removed, and existing detection-only approaches either strip clinical content, destroy temporal intervals, or break links between a patient's notes. TIDE 2.0's keyed anonymization with cryptographic surrogates and interval-preserving date shifting enables longitudinal research and patient linkage while preserving privacy, and its open license and on-premise deployment make it accessible to healthcare institutions. Surrogates are generated cryptographically with no stored linkage table; dates shift by a per-patient, interval-preserving offset; each value receives the same surrogate across all occurrences under a given key; and a release produced under a new key cannot be linked to earlier releases. The engine is open source, while the recognizer is available under a gated research-use agreement, and the paper reports recall and precision per category alongside the aggregate figures.

**Background**: De-identification is the process of removing protected health information (PHI) such as names, dates, and identifiers from clinical text so it can be used for research. It is often treated as a detection problem, but detection alone is insufficient because redaction removes clinical content along with identifiers, date blanking destroys the temporal intervals needed for longitudinal analysis, and assigning a fresh random surrogate at each occurrence breaks links between a patient's notes. Keyed anonymization instead uses a secret key to deterministically map identifiers to consistent surrogates, allowing records to remain linkable within a release while remaining unlinkable across different keys.

## [MWRL: Learning Families of Minimal Sufficient Witnesses via RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07226) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.07226) formalizes the problem of minimal-witness identification and proposes Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL credits each sampled proposal by the unique coverage it contributes to the union of certified sets, allowing a single black-box verifier bit to drive recovery of multiple minimal sufficient witnesses. Standard reinforcement learning typically converges to a single solution, so this work expands RL beyond single-solution optimization toward recovering entire families of explanations. It could benefit explainable AI, causal discovery, and any scientific or computational setting where multiple irreducible conditions jointly explain an outcome. The credit assignment is derived directly from the problem definition and unifies minimality with recovery of alternatives; the authors derive both a value-iteration planner that recovers the entire witness family and a policy-gradient method that scales to large language models. Experiments show MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, whereas baselines return redundant supersets or a single witness, and code is released at github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: A minimal sufficient witness is an irreducible set of conditions that is enough on its own to produce an observed outcome — essentially what we mean by an explanation, mechanism, or reason. In many problems there are several such witnesses, but standard RL methods tend to find only one or to return redundant supersets. A black-box verifier is an oracle that only returns a yes/no bit about whether a proposed set is sufficient, without revealing internal structure, which makes credit assignment across many proposals challenging.

## [Lineage-Aware Memory Governance for Privacy-Preserving Enterprise AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07258) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07258) introduces the Analytical Memory Unit (AMU), a memory schema that attaches a full derivation (lineage) graph to every cached result and gates retrieval so a hit is served only when the requester is authorized for every column touched. The authors prove by construction that this policy blocks retrieval of results derived from sensitive columns outside a requester's permissions, and across six experiments it removes the 18.8-25.5% cross-department leakage that naive content-gated memory suffers while keeping 81.5-82.6% of memory reuse at 13.8 microsecond worst-case overhead. Existing agent-memory systems such as MemGPT, Zep, and A-MEM gate retrieval by content, ownership, and role rather than derivation, so they can miss a cached insight that embeds a forbidden column. This framework offers a practical governance layer for shared agent memory that complements source-layer access control and supports EU AI Act compliance, making it relevant to enterprises deploying multi-department AI agents. The guarantee is conditional on complete lineage recording: eliminating measured leakage required 75-90% recorded lineage completeness, so the authors treat 90% as a conservative deployment target, and the proof excludes derived features that encode sensitive information without naming their source. A real-agent proof-of-concept with LLM-generated SQL showed zero leaks over 9 round-trips and caught two conflicts automatically, but the authors describe this as a feasibility demonstration, not evidence of production viability.

**Background**: Data lineage is the process of tracking how data is generated, transformed, transmitted, and used across systems over time, providing visibility into its life cycle and supporting auditing and compliance. Enterprise AI agents increasingly share a memory store, but current systems gate retrieval by content, ownership, and role rather than by how a cached result was derived.

## [Scale-Invariant Training Fixes Gradient Bias in Time Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07324) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07324) shows that affine scaling methods like Reversible Instance Normalization (ReVIN) cause "scale-contaminated training" (ScaleCon), where each series' gradient is multiplied by b^p (b is the scaling denominator, p the loss degree), letting high-scale series dominate gradients. The authors propose ScaleIn, which computes the loss on scaled targets, and prove it makes every mini-batch gradient and the full optimization trajectory invariant to arbitrary independent rescaling of training series. This is a fundamental flaw in how time series foundation models (TSFMs) are pretrained, and the fix is a one-line code change that lowers MASE in all 24 architecture-benchmark comparisons, with average reductions of 18.8% on GIFT-Eval and 21.9% on the M-competitions. It also improves supervised neural forecasting in 16 of 20 matched settings, so most existing forecasting pipelines can benefit immediately. The theoretical result holds for any scale-equivariant scaler and residual loss that is homogeneous of degree p, including MSE, MAE, and Quantile Loss; notably, existing TSFMs use both objectives with no consistent reporting or common convention for computing training loss. The authors isolate the convergence disparity between ScaleCon and ScaleIn in controlled studies on synthetic and real data.

## [RelayMoE Cuts Peak Memory in Distributed MoE Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07333) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces RelayMoE, a ring-based execution model for distributed Mixture-of-Experts training that avoids constructing the full top-k-expanded dispatch buffer by circulating expert weights or tokens around a ring and overlapping communication with computation. Evaluated on 30B–57B production MoE models, RelayMoE achieves a 2× average speedup over Megatron-LM in single-layer experiments and up to 2.02× higher throughput in full-model training under the same GPU memory budget. As MoE models scale to hundreds of experts and higher top-k routing, peak memory in the MoE block—not attention—becomes the dominant bottleneck, so reducing dispatch buffer memory directly enables longer sequences, larger batches, and cheaper training. This matters for systems and ML researchers building large-scale distributed training infrastructure, since the approach could be integrated into existing frameworks like Megatron-LM. RelayMoE adaptively selects between expert routing and token routing based on communication volume, and its ring structure naturally supports memory-efficient recomputation during backward passes by reconstructing expert intermediates hop-by-hop and releasing them before the next hop. The saved memory can be used for longer sequences or to retain more attention activations, reducing attention recomputation; the paper reports extending the largest tested trainable sequence length by up to 2.85×.

In distributed training, tokens must be routed to the GPUs holding their assigned experts, typically via an all-to-all collective that requires every intermediate buffer to be scaled by top-k, making memory usage grow quickly. RelayMoE instead uses a ring topology where data circulates through devices in stages, so only a fraction of the expanded buffer needs to exist at any moment.

## [RELACE: Retrospective Likelihood-Based Credit Estimation for Long-Horizon Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07349) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RELACE introduces a critic-free framework that estimates action credit by comparing teacher-forced likelihoods of executed actions under their original contexts versus outcome-augmented contexts, producing a trajectory-normalized retrospective factor that reweights discounted task returns. On ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, RELACE achieves 96.35% and 79.43% success, surpassing GiGPO by 5.47 and 5.60 percentage points respectively. Credit assignment remains a core bottleneck for training multi-turn LLM agents, where trajectory-level rewards are coarse and noisy. RELACE's fine-grained, critic-free credit estimation could improve RL training efficiency and stability for long-horizon agents without extra value or reward models, potentially influencing how future agent RL algorithms are designed. RELACE requires neither auxiliary value nor reward models nor additional autoregressive rollouts for credit estimation, and adds temporal smoothing and success-protecting masking to stabilize the local signal. It complements trajectory-level GRPO supervision by coupling retrospective relevance with observed reward, and was evaluated with both Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a critic-free RL algorithm that estimates advantages by comparing rewards within groups of rollouts for the same prompt, and it underpins models such as DeepSeek-R1. For multi-turn agents, however, GRPO's trajectory-level supervision is coarse: terminal rewards do not indicate which intermediate actions were helpful or harmful. Group-in-Group Policy Optimization (GiGPO) refines this via state-conditioned comparisons, but its credit estimates remain sensitive to downstream decisions and outcomes, motivating RELACE's retrospective likelihood-based approach.

## [AlignQuant Aligns Mixed-Precision Quantization with GPU Tiles for Faster LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07457) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07457) introduces AlignQuant, a post-training quantization method that uses GPU-compatible 2D weight tiles as the shared unit for precision allocation, compact storage, and execution. Across four LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, it achieves up to 2.50x generation speedup over BF16 while preserving model quality, with evaluations on three GPUs and contexts up to 64K tokens. Fine-grained mixed-precision quantization has long promised efficient LLM inference, but local precision choices often conflict with regular GPU storage and compute units, limiting real-world acceleration. AlignQuant shows that local precision flexibility and regular GPU execution can coexist, which could meaningfully improve LLM deployment efficiency for practitioners working on inference optimization. AlignQuant uses joint prefill/decode calibration that scores precision reductions via projection-output perturbations weighted by language-model loss gradients under quantized activations, with phase-normalized scores prioritizing tiles important to either phase under a model-wide weight-storage budget. Each tile stores one selected representation, and phase-specialized kernels reuse the packed model while expanding lower-bit weights for INT8 computation with 8-bit activations.

GPU tiles are the regular two-dimensional blocks of weights that hardware loads and computes on efficiently, so aligning quantization boundaries to these tiles is key to turning compression into actual speedups.

ElasticFit is a new VLM-guided framework that infers structured fitting cues—specifying where an object should be grounded, what volume it should occupy, how it should be oriented, and whether it should be placed rigidly, uniformly scaled, or elastically deformed—to insert objects into existing 3D scenes. In fixed-asset baseline comparisons, it improves spatial relation success from 50.8% to 69.7% and support success from 48.3% to 91.7% over the strongest baseline, while also enabling generative "make-it-fit" insertions in complex scenarios. The framework could impact 3D scene editing, AR/VR content creation, and robotics simulation by making object insertion both semantically plausible and physically consistent. ElasticFit converts high-level VLM reasoning into explicit 3D constraints that condition object generation, then generates a scene-conditioned object prior, reconstructs it in 3D, and refines the mesh through mode-specific fitting while enforcing collision avoidance, contact consistency, and physical grounding. The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2610.07460v1) and appears to be accepted at NeurIPS 2026, but no community discussion is available yet.

## [LLM-Derived Covariance Boosts Thompson Sampling for Combinatorial Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07470) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes a correlated Thompson sampling method for combinatorial semi-bandits in which an LLM is queried once to partition the arms, and that partition is converted into a positive-definite correlation matrix via an RBF kernel on cluster ranks. The correlated sampler reduces regret by 19% over standard combinatorial Thompson sampling on 16 synthetic Bernoulli families at T=2,500 and by 41% on the Microsoft MIND-small news benchmark with d=200 real articles, while still admitting a self-contained Bayesian regret bound. This work shows that LLM-provided structural priors can be injected into bandit exploration dynamics without corrupting the reward model, offering a practical way to accelerate exploration in large combinatorial action spaces. It matters for recommendation, news ranking, and other sequential decision systems where arms are numerous and correlated, and it suggests a clean separation between how a sampler moves and what it believes. The Bayesian regret bound for the idealized Gaussian sampler splits information gain into a K log T term from the K-cluster structure and a ridge term growing to d log T, so the sqrt(d/K) improvement over independent sampling is a finite-horizon transient that is exact only as within-cluster correlation tends to one. An LLM-free ablation with a simulated oracle shows that on unstructured instances the gain comes from the kernel shape rather than belief injection, and pseudo-observation warm starts provide no benefit.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Combinatorial semi-bandits are sequential decision problems where an agent selects a set of arms each round and observes the individual reward of every chosen arm, common in recommendation and ad placement. Thompson sampling is a Bayesian approach that explores by sampling from the posterior over arm rewards; the standard combinatorial version draws independent samples per arm, ignoring correlations among arms. An RBF kernel is a widely used similarity function that converts distances into covariance values, and Bayesian regret measures the expected gap between a strategy's payoff and that of the best strategy in hindsight.

On OmniNav's val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE it steers the policy toward intended low-risk actions in 84.9% and 83.2% of cases, at a cost of 6.8 and 7.9 percentage points in navigation success rate, and on a real robot it improves worst-10% average trajectory safety by 63.45% (thermal) and 32.59% (radiation) without any retraining. Safety-critical facilities such as nuclear plants or industrial sites contain hazards that RGB cameras cannot see, and the conventional fix of training a new encoder per hazard is expensive and slow. PG-VP shows that a frozen VLA model can be reused for new hazard types through visual prompting alone, which could make embodied AI deployment in hazardous environments far cheaper and more adaptable. The same virtual obstacle pattern is used regardless of hazard type, so the prompting stays fixed as new sensors are added, and nothing is rendered when no hazard is detected, meaning the policy behaves exactly as it would without PG-VP. The main caveat is the measurable drop in navigation success rate, indicating a trade-off between safety and task completion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are multimodal systems that take camera images and a natural language instruction as input and output robot actions, and they have become a major paradigm for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), where embodied agents ground instructions in visual perception to navigate 3D environments. Visual prompting is a technique that guides a pre-trained model's focus using spatial or visual cues, such as points or bounding boxes, rather than updating model weights. PG-VP combines these ideas by using physics-based risk assessment to decide an avoidance direction and then rendering a moving virtual obstacle as a visual prompt.

## [New Framework Unifies Mixtures of GFlowNets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07562) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07562) introduces a general theoretical framework for mixtures of GFlowNets, splitting them into continuously indexed (CI) and discretely indexed (DI) collections. It also proposes Stratum-Conditioned (SC) GFlowNets, which decompose the state space via a modular function and support embarrassingly parallel training without extra computation. This work provides a unified conceptual foundation for ensemble-based GFlowNet training, which has become a common but poorly understood technique for improving exploration and convergence. The proposed SC GFlowNets could make ensemble sampling more practical by speeding up convergence and mode coverage without runtime overhead, benefiting researchers in probabilistic inference and generative modeling. CI GFlowNets are interpreted through random features expansion, provably boosting expressivity in graph-structured tasks and reducing learning instability via spectral shifting. DI GFlowNets encompass prior GFlowNet training approaches and inspire SC GFlowNets, which are based on Doob's h-transform of Markov chains and restrict each component to sample from a distinct subset of the state space.

**Background**: GFlowNets (Generative Flow Networks) are a class of generative models that learn a stochastic policy to sample compositional objects (e.g., graphs or molecules) with probability proportional to a given reward function. Training an ensemble of GFlowNets, rather than a single monolithic sampler, has become a popular way to improve state-space exploration and convergence, but the theoretical connection between these ensemble methods has remained unclear. This paper addresses that gap by providing a formal framework and a new ensemble variant.

## [Latent Disturbance Modeling Enables Robust World Model Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07599) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07599) introduces a method that models latent-space disturbances as perturbations to learned latent dynamics, constructing an uncertainty set via a dynamics-aware similarity metric, out-of-distribution detection, and conformal prediction calibration. The approach jointly optimizes robust robot actions and worst-case latent disturbances through game-theoretic optimization, reducing failures by 70% in latent safety filtering and 54% in sampling-based policy steering on a Franka manipulator. This work addresses a fundamental challenge in applying robust optimization to learned latent spaces of world models, where disturbances cannot be directly defined from high-dimensional observations. It could significantly improve safety and reliability in robotics and AI safety applications that rely on world models for decision-making under uncertainty. The uncertainty set is calibrated using conformal prediction to keep imagined transitions plausible without becoming overly pessimistic, and the method is evaluated in both controlled simulations and hardware experiments with a Franka manipulator. The approach supports two paradigms: latent safety filtering and sample-and-verify steering of a generative control policy.

**Background**: World models are learned neural network models that simulate environment dynamics, allowing reinforcement learning agents to plan and learn from imagined rollouts with high sample efficiency. Robust optimization is a mathematical framework for selecting actions that remain effective under worst-case disturbances, but applying it to learned latent spaces is difficult because the latent state space and dynamics are inferred from high-dimensional observations rather than explicitly specified. Conformal prediction is a statistical technique that provides calibrated uncertainty sets with finite-sample guarantees.

## [Linear Fitness Subspace Enables Sample-Efficient Protein Directed Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07607) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An arXiv preprint (2610.07607) proposes the Linear Fitness Subspace (LFS) hypothesis, arguing that mutation-induced residue-level representation changes in protein language models contain a compact, assay-specific set of directions along which fitness varies linearly from only a few labeled variants. Building on this, the authors introduce Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES), which estimates an LFS from a small initial sample and performs surrogate modeling, uncertainty estimation, and acquisition within that learned subspace. Model-guided directed evolution is bottlenecked by the cost of wet-lab oracle evaluations, so a method that improves sample efficiency could substantially reduce experimental burden in protein engineering. SGES reportedly outperforms zero-shot protein language models and recent ML-guided protein optimization baselines across 10 core ProteinGym assays, 87 extended static-validation assays, and an 18-assay budgeted-search evaluation, suggesting practical value for AI-driven protein design. The LFS claim is explicitly framed as a local, supervision-recoverable statement rather than a universal claim that protein fitness landscapes or global PLM geometry are linear. Controlled comparisons against PCA, random projections, label-shuffled PLS, classical mutation features, and acquisition ablations isolate the benefit of the fitness-aligned site-delta coordinate, though the work remains a preprint without peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Directed evolution mimics natural selection in the lab by iterating mutagenesis, selection, and amplification to steer proteins toward a desired function, but each round requires costly experimental assays. Protein language models (pLMs) are transformer-based models trained on vast protein sequence databases, analogous to LLMs trained on text, and provide rich representations that can score variants without task-specific labels. Model-guided directed evolution uses such models as surrogates to propose promising variants under a limited oracle budget, but zero-shot scores may be misaligned with the target assay and supervised search in high-dimensional embedding spaces tends to be sample-inefficient.

## [LORE-KV: Monte Carlo Estimation for Future-Aware KV Cache Eviction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07643) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced LORE-KV, a training-free KV-cache eviction method that samples short autoregressive continuations from the frozen target model and uses their response-side query states to estimate prompt-token utility via projected leave-one-out attention-output deletion costs. At a cache budget of B=128, it raised the LongBench average on Qwen2.5-14B from 45.49 to 48.24 and the 16K RULER average on Mistral-7B from 45.20 to 51.05. KV-cache memory is a first-order bottleneck for long-context LLM deployment, and LORE-KV reframes eviction as estimating which memory will matter during answering rather than which appeared important while reading the prompt. Its training-free, auxiliary-model-free design could make future-aware eviction practical for existing dense and hybrid-attention backbones. Ablations show that at B=128 a single response-side continuation recovers about 89% of the gain over the prompt-window control, with additional sampled futures yielding smaller improvements; gains diminish at larger cache budgets and coexist with task-level regressions. The method incurs 1.46–2.77x AnDPro's per-sample wall-clock time as a one-time compression overhead across six dense and hybrid-attention backbones.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: KV caching stores key and value tensors for every token in the context so that autoregressive decoding does not recompute attention over the whole prompt at each step, but the cache grows linearly with sequence length and can exhaust GPU memory. Eviction methods therefore drop less important tokens under a fixed budget, and most prior approaches judge importance from the prompt alone, even though decoding queries are unavailable at eviction time. Monte Carlo estimation refers to approximating a quantity by repeated random sampling, and leave-one-out deletion cost measures how much a model's output changes when a single token is removed.

## [SkillPoison: Poisoning LLM Agent Skills via Verified Successful Experiences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07645) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce SkillPoison, a framework that progressively poisons self-improving LLM agents by constructing successful experiences that reinforce a target behavior and then removing the contextual constraints on when that behavior applies. Across three benchmarks, SkillPoison achieves a 95.71% attack success rate while every injected experience remains task-correct and passes verification and lexical inspection. This reveals a subtle security gap in self-improving agent pipelines: poisoning no longer requires any malicious trajectory, so existing defenses that scan individual experiences or extracted skills for malicious content may fail. It matters for anyone deploying agents that distill experience into reusable skills, since a poisoned skill can stay dormant and only cause harm when misapplied. Rather than injecting malicious content, SkillPoison shapes how the skill extractor generalizes, letting a useful behavior support task success while inducing harmful behavior when misapplied. The attack is notable because all injected experiences are task-correct and survive verification and lexical inspection, and the code, data, and implementation details are released at the DEEP-JLU/SkillPoison GitHub repository.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly distill successful experiences into persistent, reusable skills, so that lessons from past trajectories can guide future behavior. Prior skill attacks corrupt this pipeline by injecting malicious triggers, behaviors, or false facts into individual experiences or extracted skills, but such attacks are relatively easy to detect and the injected behaviors often fail to accumulate as persistent skills. SkillPoison instead exploits the generalization step of skill extraction, showing that poisoning can emerge even from verified successful experiences.

## [Exact-Solution Volume Explains Length Generalization in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07676) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces normalized exact-solution volume (NESV), the fraction of a bounded parameter region that exactly solves a task for every input of length n, and derives asymptotic bounds for fixed-width, single-layer transformers with log n-scaled attention on four tasks: FIRST (Θ(1)), MAJORITY (Θ(1/(n log n))), INDEX (Θ(1/n^3)), and PARITY (0). It further shows that a modified transformer structurally eliminating one error source in INDEX improves the NESV bound to Θ(n^{-1}) and achieves 85% accuracy at 10x training length versus 60% for the original model. This work bridges transformer expressivity and generalization by linking how quickly the exact-solution volume decays with input length to how hard a task is to length-generalize, offering a theoretical tool that matches prior empirical findings. It could help researchers diagnose concrete sources of length sensitivity and guide task-specific model refinements for applications requiring processing of sequences longer than those seen during training. The analysis is limited to fixed-width, single-layer transformers with log n-scaled attention, and the NESV bounds are asymptotic rather than finite-sample guarantees. For INDEX, the volume analysis identifies two error sources that grow with n; the improved model eliminates one structurally, improving the theoretical bound and empirical accuracy at 10x length, though the other error source remains.

**Background**: Transformers are the dominant neural architecture for sequence tasks, but they are typically trained on fixed-length inputs and often fail to generalize to longer sequences at test time. Prior theoretical work on transformer expressivity shows whether a transformer can represent a solution to a task, but says little about whether a learned solution will extend to longer inputs. Length generalization is the ability to accurately process strings longer than those seen during training, and understanding it is important for practical deployment on variable-length data.

## [SanSi: A Looped Typed Decision Model for System 1.5 Thinking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07730) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SanSi introduces a looped typed decision model that recursively applies the same layers several times before a single typed readout, refining hidden states without generating any text. On 10,027 test decisions from 59 sources, it reaches 72.0% accuracy, 13.5 points above a non-looped model of the same shape and 1.8 points below a model with three times the parameters. This work carves out a middle ground between fast single-pass System 1 decisions and slow text-generating System 2 reasoning, showing that looping can buy substantial accuracy at low parameter cost. It could influence future research on efficient reasoning and on typed decision models used as judges or guardrails. Option probabilities are read after every loop and each loop is trained with a proper scoring rule, so a single model serves every budget from one to eight loops in one run. On two depth-controlled tasks, loops extend the solvable depth beyond training depths where a larger single-pass model fails, and as an RL judge without gold answers SanSi raises the generator's F1 by 7.7 points.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Typed decision models answer a declared question without generating text: a decision head returns a probability for each declared option in a single forward pass, which is fast, intuitive System 1 thinking. Looped language models reuse the same parameter-shared transformer layers repeatedly to simulate deeper computation with fewer parameters. SanSi combines these ideas, turning a pre-trained looped language model into a typed decision model and calling the intermediate regime System 1.5 thinking.

## [RELER: Reinforcement Learning for Dense Retrieval in Embedding Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07731) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced RELER (REinforcement Learning for Retrieval), a framework that trains existing dense retrieval embedding models directly in embedding space by sampling unit-length query and document embeddings from von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distributions and updating the encoder with REINFORCE using a leave-one-out baseline (RLOO). A conditional-mean projection (CMP) step reduces sampling noise in the high-dimensional policy gradient, and RELER consistently outperforms InfoNCE and LambdaLoss in average nDCG@10 when post-training BGE-M3 and Qwen3-Embedding backbones on the BRIGHT benchmark. Dense retrieval models are usually trained with contrastive objectives that learn good representations but do not directly optimize retrieval metrics or downstream task performance, so RELER's ability to align embeddings with task-specific rewards could improve both retrieval quality and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answer quality. This matters for information retrieval and representation learning researchers and practitioners who rely on embedding models for search and RAG pipelines. RELER samples unit-length query and document embedding actions from von Mises-Fisher distributions centered on normalized encoder outputs, scores retrieval or downstream outcomes as rewards, and updates the encoder with RLOO; the proposed conditional-mean projection projects each sampled embedding onto the low-dimensional subspace spanned by its encoder output and the candidate embeddings it is compared against, reducing policy-gradient noise while preserving its expectation. In RAG experiments, only the query encoder is adapted while the document index and generator stay fixed, and jointly optimizing retrieval and answer rewards across seven QA datasets improves both average retrieval performance and answer quality.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Dense retrieval represents queries and documents as vectors (embeddings) and finds relevant documents by measuring similarity in that embedding space, typically training encoders with contrastive losses such as InfoNCE. Reinforcement learning from task rewards offers an alternative that directly optimizes what we care about, but exploring a high-dimensional embedding space is noisy. The von Mises-Fisher distribution is the natural probability distribution over directions on a sphere, making it well suited for sampling normalized embeddings, while RLOO (REINFORCE leave-one-out) is a policy-gradient technique that reduces variance by comparing each sample's reward against the average reward of the other samples in its group.

## [Cleave decouples algebraic search and operator scheduling for tensor kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07742) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Cleave is a new ML compiler that uses symbolic decoupling to separate algebraic transformation from operator scheduling, generating kernels up to 2.8x faster than the best baseline (1.6x on average) and reducing compilation time by 5.9x on average compared to Mirage. It also achieves geometric mean speedups of 1.4x and 1.7x over FlashInfer's handwritten FA2 and FA3 backends on dynamic production workloads. This approach could enable ML compilers to automatically generate highly optimized kernels like FlashAttention that previously required expert hand-writing, potentially reducing engineering effort and improving performance for large language model inference and training. It addresses a key bottleneck in ML systems where compilers struggle to match handwritten kernel efficiency. Cleave represents shapes as symbols to make equivalence checking cheap and introduces a new Split operator with a symbolic split count to parallelize along reduction dimensions. Its scheduler fuses graphs with multiple reductions through iterative tiling and horizontal fusion, and the code is available at https://github.com/nyu-systems/cleave.

## [Late-Concentrated Token Reduction Schedule Boosts ViT Robustness Under Distribution Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07758) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a one-parameter late-concentrated power-law schedule for training-free token reduction in vision transformers, which consistently improves out-of-distribution accuracy over the standard flat schedule at no extra inference cost. On ImageNet-C with DeiT-S, the late schedule closes 83% of the accuracy gap to the uncompressed model at a 26% compute reduction (+1.17pp) and 99% of the gap at a lighter 7% reduction (+0.26pp). This finding is significant because token reduction is widely used for efficient ViT deployment, but its robustness under real-world distribution shift has been largely overlooked. The simple schedule change requires no retraining, no per-input tuning, and no extra compute, making it immediately applicable to existing efficient inference pipelines and safety-critical applications where corrupted inputs are common. The gain cannot be attributed to retaining more tokens or using extra compute: when held to the flat schedule's compute budget, the late schedule removes more tokens in total and leaves fewer tokens at the end, yet still wins. Single-layer probes suggest the mechanism is that earlier reductions perturb features that pass through more remaining layers, front-loading reduction error in depth; the effect holds across five token-reduction methods (ToMe, EViT, ATS, ATC, PiToMe), nine backbones, all ImageNet-C corruption types, eight further shift suites, and two further modalities (video and vision-language QA).

The paper introduces OFAG, a foundation model for attributed graph clustering that is trained once on synthetic attributed graphs and then applied directly to diverse real-world graphs without any graph-specific training, fine-tuning, or hyperparameter search. HERMES instantiates these primitives via a dependency-aware dynamic activation mechanism and a bug diagnosis mechanism that maps execution evidence back to the components that must be revised; the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [ReFold: Training-Free Reversible Context Folding for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07863) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReFold introduces a training-free rendering layer that compresses the model's rendered context for long-horizon LLM agents by removing two kinds of inter-turn redundancy — content already shown in earlier turns (replaced by a stub) and turns the agent reports as finished (folded into a one-line note) — without any auxiliary predictor. Evaluated across five long-horizon benchmarks and two frontier LLMs, it cuts token consumption by up to 2.5x, halves KV-cache memory per session, and avoids up to 92% of forced compactions without degrading task success rates. Context window growth is a central bottleneck for long-horizon agents, and existing predictive compression methods add runtime overhead, invalidate prefix caches, and permanently discard content. ReFold's reversible, rendering-layer approach is plug-and-play across standard ReAct-style harnesses and, under concurrent serving workloads, reduces request queuing delays by up to 100%, accelerates inference by up to 1.7x, and cuts inference costs by up to 3.4x. Both folding operators use chunked rendering, rewriting the cached prefix once every few steps rather than at every step, and every removal is strictly reversible — a wrong removal costs one restore from the preserved interaction history rather than permanent content loss. Because it operates at the rendering layer, the underlying append-only interaction history is fully preserved and the method requires no training or auxiliary model calls.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Long-horizon LLM agents act on an append-only interaction history that is re-sent to the model at every step, so context length and cost grow with the number of steps until sessions exceed the context window. Existing approaches manage this via context requirement prediction, relying on extra model calls, heuristic rules, or trained policies, which introduce runtime overhead and invalidate prefix caches — the KV cache blocks reused for recurring prompt prefixes. ReFold instead compresses only the rendered context while keeping the full history intact, making it compatible with prefix caching and standard agent harnesses.

## [CMC Uses Stochastic Optimal Control to Curb Content Leakage in Video Motion Customization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07911) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07911v1) proposes Control-based Motion Customization (CMC), a training framework that formulates motion customization as a Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC) problem to prevent generative dynamics from collapsing toward the reference video. The method eliminates the need for an explicit reward and introduces a timestep-adaptive motion cost focused only on early generative stages, accelerating training by 2.5 times. Content leakage — where appearance attributes from a reference video bleed into generated outputs — is a persistent obstacle in video motion customization, and CMC's principled control-theoretic formulation offers a structurally robust alternative to direct regression objectives. If validated, this could improve motion fidelity and diversity for text-to-video customization pipelines used in content creation and VFX. The SOC formulation steers customized videos to acquire the target motion while remaining within the pre-trained model's prompt-conditional distribution, so appearance is governed by the text prompt rather than the reference video. The timestep-adaptive motion cost focuses only on early generative stages, and experiments report competitive motion fidelity with preserved base-model diversity, though the work is a preprint without peer review or community engagement metrics.

## [Hybrid Latent Attention Cuts Looped LLM KV Cache by 10.7x](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07940) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Hybrid Latent Attention (HLA), which keeps exact keys and values only within a sliding window of W recent tokens and stores older tokens as compact latents that each loop's query reads directly, without reconstructing keys and values. Uptrained on Ouro looped models (T=4) at 1.4B and 2.6B parameters with pretrained weights frozen, HLA shrinks the per-token cache by 10.7x, fits 4.0-8.8x more concurrent sequences per GPU, and speeds decoding by 2.5x at 1K context and up to 7.4x at 16K. Looped language models deepen computation without adding parameters, but their KV cache grows by a factor of T, which directly limits batch size and decoding speed on GPUs. HLA shows this memory penalty can be largely removed with minimal accuracy loss, making looped architectures far more practical for high-throughput inference and long-context serving. HLA retains over 97% of original accuracy on math, knowledge, and reasoning benchmarks and 96-100% on long-context retrieval up to 16K tokens, and after supervised fine-tuning it matches the fine-tuned original model on competition-level math. The approach only trains the added parameters while keeping pretrained weights frozen, so it acts as a lightweight uptraining procedure rather than a full retraining.

**Background**: Looped language models such as Ouro apply the same stack of transformer layers T times to each token, gaining deeper iterative computation in latent space without increasing parameter count. The KV cache is a standard inference optimization that stores past tokens' key and value vectors so they are not recomputed at each generation step, but in looped models this cache is multiplied by T, making it a major memory and bandwidth bottleneck. HLA addresses this by combining exact attention over a recent sliding window with compressed latent representations for older tokens.

## [SALT Enables Self-Supervised Test-Time Adaptation for VLA Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07946) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT), a method that lets vision-language-action (VLA) policies adapt to unknown visual disruptions during execution using only their own leftover, unexecuted action chunks as supervision. On LIBERO-10, SALT raised average success across five persistent visual corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while a real robot's task progress improved from 0.49 to 0.61. Robots deployed in the real world frequently encounter unexpected visual disruptions such as lighting changes, occlusions, or camera shifts, and SALT addresses this practical challenge without requiring disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations. This could make VLA-based manipulation more robust and deployable in unstructured environments, benefiting robotics researchers and practitioners working on real-world autonomy. SALT exploits the temporal overlap between consecutive action chunks: the leftover from the previous chunk provides a temporally aligned target for the current prediction, enabling Transition Anchoring at the onset of a visual shift and Sequential Correction Propagation at each replan. A lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories decides when updates begin, and the method largely preserves nominal performance.

## [ReGraph models how generalization emerges from dual visual streams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07962) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ReGraph, a recurrent dual-stream graph model with biological inductive biases (retina-driven stream-specialized encoding, dorsal-to-ventral modulation, and dynamic lateral connectivity), trained on the Something-Something V2 action benchmark. The model showed that context-invariant codes and grid-like spatial bases uniquely co-emerged along the extended dorsal stream, and post-hoc analyses revealed these grid-like bases act as reusable routing templates via lateral connectivity. This work bridges neuroscience and AI by offering a computational account of how generalization capacity—extracting context-invariant relational structures—may not emerge abruptly in a dedicated region like the hippocampus, but rather takes shape as sensory information is parsed into factorized dorsal 'where' and ventral 'what' streams. It suggests that biological inductive biases are prerequisites for relational learning, which could inform the design of more generalizable AI architectures. ReGraph incorporates retina-driven stream-specialized encoding, dorsal-to-ventral modulation, and dynamic lateral connectivity, and was trained on the Something-Something V2 action benchmark. The absence of context-invariant codes and grid-like bases in single-stream, unmodulated variants and standard baselines implies that these inductive biases are necessary for the emergence of relational structures.

**Background**: The dual-stream hypothesis in neuroscience posits that visual information splits into a dorsal 'where' pathway for spatial and motion processing and a ventral 'what' pathway for object recognition. Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) fire in a hexagonal pattern and provide context-invariant spatial codes, and similar grid-like patterns have been observed in neocortical regions along the dorsal pathway. Graph neural networks are models that operate on graph-structured data and are known to have inductive biases that shape what they learn, making them suitable for modeling relational structures in the brain.

## [Paper Formalizes Cost-Accuracy Optimization for Semantic Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08089) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08089) gives a formal problem definition for cost-accuracy optimization in semantic query engines, using the calibrated confidence that decision models such as Jev attach to each decision to estimate expected output quality without any labeled data. It defines oracle semantics for relational algebra with semantic operators, physical plans as logical plan plus decision policy pairs, declarative output-level targets, and a hierarchy of plan equivalence. Existing semantic query systems either apply a fixed threshold per operator or tune accuracy per operator, ignoring how errors propagate through joins; this framework fills that gap and could let query optimizers pick plans that meet accuracy targets at lower cost. It matters for database and ML systems researchers and practitioners building semantic query engines on top of machine-learned predicates. The paper shows accuracy is plan-invariant under pointwise-deterministic policies, that selection pushdown is not quality-sound when escalation bands are calibrated on the plan's own candidates, and that expected quality is computable in polynomial time under bag semantics while under set semantics it follows the dichotomy of tuple-independent probabilistic databases. Choosing which tuples to drop is NP-hard, but the optimization decomposes into per-tuple decisions via two Lagrange multipliers, and the evaluation is limited to simulations on a synthetic workload with real-engine evaluation left for future work.

## [When Tools Lie: How Mathematical Agents Handle Corrupted Tool Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08097) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08097) introduces a controlled corruption framework in which a hidden interceptor replaces tool call results with plausible but incorrect information on targeted math problems. Testing 31 problems across four verification designs, the authors find accuracy drops from 100% to 72.4% without verification, while mandatory same-context reflection fully restores accuracy to 100%. The findings show that verifier availability and verification policy are separate components of agent reliability, meaning teams cannot assume that simply providing a verification tool will protect against silent tool failures. This has direct implications for the design of mathematical and tool-using AI agents, where optional verification only helps if the model actually chooses to invoke it. The study evaluated four designs—no verification, mandatory same-context reflection, optional fresh-context verification, and optional structural verification—and found that checking frequency strongly correlates with robustness, while unequal invocation rates prevented a controlled comparison of verifier quality. A supporting recovery experiment showed that a full problem restart succeeded in 100% of cases after explicit detection of corruption.

A new arXiv paper (2610.08153) introduces penalty-framed no-valid-option MCQA, a setting in which the labeled correct option is removed from MMLU-Pro math questions and models must either pick a remaining choice or output ABSTAIN, with invalid forced choices penalized. The authors also propose correct-conditioned analysis, evaluating abstention only on instances the model originally answered correctly, and find that even with explicit no-valid-option instructions and penalty-based scoring, models still make invalid forced-choice responses on a subset of those instances. This work exposes a failure mode that standard answer-selection accuracy completely misses: a model can score highly on MCQA benchmarks yet still refuse to abstain when no option is actually correct, which matters for safe deployment in retrieval-augmented and user-facing systems where invalid option sets can occur. The experiments use the mathematics subset of MMLU-Pro, a benchmark that expanded the original MMLU from four to ten answer choices with more reasoning-focused questions, and the evaluation penalizes invalid forced-choice responses while allowing ABSTAIN as an output. The correct-conditioned analysis is a notable methodological choice because it isolates abstention behavior from general question-answering ability, though the abstract is truncated and does not report specific model names or quantitative abstention rates.

S1-MAS uses a lightweight controller that selects inspection conditions, chooses subsequent tasks, and determines termination, plus a compact reader that retrieves condition-relevant evidence from authorized sources, forming a decision-evidence loop that dynamically assigns worker roles and source access without task-specific training. ## [GeoPID: Training-Free Geometric Steering of Visual Information in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08401) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose GeoPID, a training-free framework that decomposes multimodal representations in vision-language models into Redundant, Modality-Unique, and Synergistic components based on the geometric relationships between visual and textual subspaces. Building on this analysis across 22 VLMs and 14 benchmarks, they introduce an inference-time intervention that amplifies visual representations along the vision-unique subspace, achieving an average relative accuracy gain of 7.63% without updating any model parameters. Vision-language models are known to under-use visual information and over-rely on textual context, which hurts tasks requiring genuine visual grounding. GeoPID shows this weakness can be mitigated at inference time without retraining, making it a lightweight, broadly applicable tool for improving multimodal reliability across many existing models. The method is entirely training-free and requires no additional model parameters, operating purely by steering representations along the vision-unique subspace during inference. The analysis confirms that correct predictions exhibit stronger vision-unique components specifically when questions strongly demand visual grounding, and the reported 7.63% gain is an average relative improvement across 14 benchmarks.

## [Probing Unanswerability Signals Across Domains and Multi-Turn Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08413) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a turn-labeled multi-turn benchmark of 423 conversations and 1,661 labeled turn-states, plus an evaluation harness with a simulated user who answers clarifying questions, and uses them with six datasets and six open-weight LLMs to test how far probes for unanswerability transfer. It finds that probes transfer robustly between datasets sharing a ground of unanswerability, such as missing information in math (AUROC 0.77-0.97) and in a passage (SQuAD 2.0<->MuSiQue, 0.77-0.90), but single-turn probes fail zero-shot to detect when a conversation becomes answerable. This work matters because large language models routinely answer questions that cannot be answered from the given information, and in dialogue they answer before enough has been said, so understanding whether unanswerability signals generalize across domains and turns is key to building more reliable and honest AI systems. It provides both a benchmark and a transferability analysis that could inform future work on clarification-seeking and abstention behavior in LLMs. Probes for epistemic "known-unknowns" transfer poorly to math, but this separation weakens under lexical controls and changes with layer and coordinate system, so it remains unresolved; a gate on the calibrated probe fires on underspecified turns far more precisely than chance and its end-task success comes within 0.08 of a gate given true labels, yet across four models it does not reliably beat vanilla generation or prompted consolidation. The remaining gap lies mostly in how models use a clarification, not in detection.

## [Cross-Tokenizer Distillation: Alignment Coverage Isn't the Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08448) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08448) shows that in cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD), strict 1:1 alignment already covers most student-generated tokens across three heterogeneous teacher-student pairs on math reasoning and code generation. Restricting reverse KL to a student-selected top-16 subset of the shared vocabulary at strict positions matches full shared-vocabulary OPD accuracy, while adding MSE supervision on span log-probabilities in mismatch groups gives complete coverage but reduces accuracy. This challenges the common assumption that expanding alignment coverage between mismatched tokenizers improves distillation, suggesting researchers should instead prioritize supervision reliability. It could redirect future cross-tokenizer distillation work away from heuristic alignment-expansion methods toward compact, high-confidence supervision signals. The paper reports that on pre-distillation student samples, the shared vocabulary retains nearly all teacher and student probability mass at strictly aligned positions on average. Diagnostics show that span gradients from the strict-only loss have weak or negative directional agreement with strict gradients and grow in magnitude, which may explain the accuracy drop when span supervision is added.

## [MetaLearnNCA: Gradient-Free Few-Shot Meta-Learning via Interacting Neural Cellular Automata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08479) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MetaLearnNCA introduces a decentralized few-shot meta-learning framework that adapts to new tasks through the dynamical interaction of coupled Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs) without computing analytical gradients during inference. It decomposes adaptation into an Active-NCA that performs task inference on a continuous 2D spatial memory grid (the spatial program) and a Meta-NCA that acts as a decentralized cellular optimizer by diffusing spatial error residuals across local neighborhoods. This work shows that robust, gradient-free learning-to-learn can emerge from decentralized cellular dynamics on non-von Neumann substrates, potentially avoiding the costly test-time backpropagation that plagues traditional gradient-based meta-learners. It also preserves native 2D spatial geometry, which metric-based methods typically discard by flattening features into 1D vectors. MetaLearnNCA achieves 96.12% in-distribution on Omniglot and shows out-of-distribution transfer gains across MNIST, KMNIST, and Fashion-MNIST over 10 independent testing seeds in 1-, 5-, and 10-shot regimes, surpassing Prototypical Networks by +10.54% on 10-shot MNIST and FOMAML by +3.87% on 10-shot Fashion-MNIST. The framework operates offline and relies on local neighborhood interactions rather than global gradient computation.

**Background**: Neural Cellular Automata (NCA) are models that combine neural networks with the principles of cellular automata, where a grid of cells updates its states based on local neighbor interactions, enabling self-organizing and regenerative pattern formation. Few-shot meta-learning aims to let models generalize to new tasks from only a few examples, traditionally via gradient-based optimization through unrolled graphs or metric-based comparisons on flattened feature vectors. FlowCF is a new model-agnostic generative method that frames counterfactual explanation generation as sparse transport from a factual input to a target class, solved with flow matching extended to mixed feature types via a novel mixed flow operator. On six benchmark datasets it achieves the best numerical sparsity and proximity, changing only 29% of numerical features versus 89% for the best baseline, with 70% smaller displacement. The method exploits the geometry of the learned flow and uses a gating network to minimize the number of features the transport modifies, while remaining comparable to baselines on other desiderata. A new arXiv preprint (2610.08544) proposes reading every interpretability probe score against two reference points: a floor, what a declared set of simple inputs already predicts, and a ceiling, what the full input can predict. ## [Latent space bias directions in LLMs capture confidence, not fairness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08559) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.08559) analyzes the linear debiasing direction used in activation steering for large language models and finds that this direction is dominated by model confidence rather than encoding a meaningful representation of bias. Steering along it reduces measured bias only because it lowers model confidence, causing the model to abstain from answering on QA benchmarks. This challenges a popular lightweight debiasing technique and explains its inconsistent performance, with important implications for researchers working on LLM alignment, interpretability, and AI safety. It suggests that steering-based debiasing results should be interpreted with care, since apparent fairness gains may simply reflect reduced model confidence. The study contrasts activations of anti-biased and biased prompts to obtain the linear debiasing direction, then evaluates it as a steering intervention across bias and general knowledge benchmarks. It finds that model confidence is the dominant separating factor between biased and anti-biased prompts in hidden space, making it difficult to isolate a linear bias representation disentangled from confidence.

## [Information-Theoretic Framework Locates When Diffusion Features Emerge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08626) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces feature information dynamics, an information-theoretic framework that uses the I-MMSE identity to connect the rate of change of a feature's mutual information to the gap between optimal unconditional and feature-conditional denoising losses, yielding practical estimators for feature information density. It also develops a chained decomposition separating shared from incremental information in a feature hierarchy, and applies the framework to quantitatively confirm spectral autoregression in pixel diffusion and to analyze a class → mask → Canny conditioning chain across pixel, SDVAE, VAVAE, and RAE representations. This work turns the widely observed but qualitative intuition that diffusion models generate coarse structure before fine detail into a quantitative, information-theoretic measurement, giving researchers a principled tool to study when and how features emerge. Its finding that per-feature information densities differ across representations suggests that ordered generation could improve diffusion training, with implications for generative modeling and representation learning. The framework relies on the I-MMSE identity to relate mutual information to minimum mean-square error, and the resulting estimators are practical because they only require comparing unconditional and feature-conditional denoising losses. The analysis is demonstrated on pixel diffusion and on a hierarchical class → mask → Canny conditioning chain, with code released at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/feature-information-dynamics.

Reading a chat model outside its chat template reverses the sign of the gap with nothing at stake (-0.038 versus +0.055 under the template on OLMo-3), and on both models that carry the gap, reasoning about the stakes before acting shifts choices back toward the model's own judgment.

## [RLCP Adapts Action Sets in Sequential Recommendation via Conformal Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08743) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.08743) proposes Reinforcement Learning with Calibrated Pruning (RLCP), which dynamically adjusts the retained action set in sequential recommendation using critic scores and an online threshold updated from binary feedback. The authors prove a deterministic bound on the proxy miss rate along adaptive trajectories and derive an exact decomposition of value loss into filtering and selection losses, with experiments on KuaiRand-Pure and MovieLens 1M showing RLCP variants achieve the highest catalog diversity in all 19 configurations, reaching 1.11x to 5.21x that of the strongest baseline. Most sequential recommenders use a fixed slate size even though the number of useful alternatives varies within a session, so RLCP's adaptive pruning could improve both diversity and efficiency in reinforcement learning-based recommendation. The theoretical guarantees on miss rate and reward bounds make the approach more trustworthy for deployment, and the results suggest it could be adopted by researchers and practitioners working on RL-driven recommender systems. The online threshold is updated from binary feedback indicating whether the retained set contains an action in a proxy target, and the finite session reward bound accounts for imperfect selection and set truncation without requiring learning parameters to converge. Experiments compare two RLCP implementations against four RL baselines, with RLCP achieving competitive session depth and no larger retained sets.

The paper introduces Universe of Thoughts (UoT), a framework that formalizes combinational, exploratory, and transformational creativity as executable computational operators over structured problem and solution spaces, and instantiates them as LLM reasoning methods. UoT distinguishes three modes: combinational reasoning transfers ideas across domains, exploratory reasoning searches within an existing conceptual space, and transformational reasoning modifies the rules or constraints defining that space. Results indicate T-UoT is strongest in low-constraint, high-objective-specificity settings, E-UoT in more constrained, high-specificity settings, and C-UoT in low-constraint, lower-specificity settings; the work is a preprint without community discussion yet.

## [Von Neumann Networks: Learnable Neuron Roles on Cellular Arrays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05780) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Von Neumann Networks (VNNs), a neural architecture where each artificial neuron occupies a cell on a cellular array and learns a specialized role, echoing John von Neumann's mid-20th-century cellular automaton model of the brain. The authors construct a mathematical framework showing VNNs extend neural operators and learn Green's functions via convolutions on a diffusion-signature cellular topology, and prove they belong to a computationally universal class called Cellular Machines. This work bridges classic cellular automata theory with modern deep learning, offering a self-engineered architecture whose design depends only on the placement of inputs and outputs on the cellular array. If the initial results hold, VNN-based models could deliver better parameter efficiency than equivalent MLPs and open new directions for neural operators and PDE-related learning tasks. Initial experiments show VNN-based multi-layered perceptrons outperform equivalent deep learning variants on basic tasks while using fewer parameters, and they can learn new task types, including extending the von Neumann hardware architecture to cells. The universality claim rests on VNNs being a subset of Cellular Machines, though the paper is a v2 arXiv preprint and results remain preliminary.

**Background**: Von Neumann cellular automata, developed in the 1940s with Stanislaw Ulam, model computation as an array of cells each in one of finitely many states, originally to study machine self-replication. Neural operators are deep learning architectures that learn mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces, often as fast surrogates for solving partial differential equations. Green's functions describe the response of a linear system to a point source and are central to solving such equations, so learning them with convolutions connects the new architecture to established operator-learning theory.

## [XDecomposer: Prior-Free Set Decomposition for Multiphase X-ray Diffraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05866) ⭐️ 7.0/10

XDecomposer introduces a prior-free framework that jointly decomposes and identifies multiphase powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns without requiring candidate phase lists, structural templates, or prior knowledge of the number of phases. It formulates multiphase diffraction analysis as a set prediction problem, inferring an unordered set of phase-resolved components, their mixture proportions, and structural representations within a unified architecture, with code openly available on GitHub. Multiphase PXRD analysis is a long-standing bottleneck in materials science, since real-world synthesis often yields complex mixtures that cannot be reliably disentangled. By removing the dependence on prior-guided iterative phase matching, XDecomposer offers a practical route toward data-driven, source-resolved multiphase XRD analysis that could accelerate automated materials characterization and self-driving materials discovery. The framework combines a phase-query-driven decomposition mechanism with diffraction-consistent physical reconstruction to achieve accurate source separation while preserving crystallographic fidelity. Experiments on both simulated and experimental datasets show substantially improved reconstruction accuracy and phase identification across diverse chemical systems, with strong generalization to unseen mixtures.

**Background**: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is a core technique for identifying crystalline phases and determining unit cell dimensions by analyzing finely ground, homogenized samples. Traditional phase identification relies on matching patterns against reference databases and iterative refinement methods such as Rietveld analysis, which become unreliable when multiple phases overlap. Recent deep-learning approaches have shown promise for single-phase inputs but break down in multiphase settings, motivating prior-free methods like XDecomposer.

## [PAGE Probe Finds LoRA Works Best in One Shallow FFN Module](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06183) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces PAGE (Projected Adapter Gradient Energy), a gradient-based sensitivity probe that estimates the initial trainable gradient energy available to each candidate LoRA adapter. Surprisingly, PAGE is highly concentrated on a single shallow FFN down-projection across two model families and four downstream tasks, which the authors term the 'dominant adaptation module', and they propose DomLoRA, which places a single adapter there and outperforms vanilla LoRA with only 0.7% of its trainable parameters. This finding challenges the common practice of broadly distributing LoRA adapters and offers a practical placement guideline that could substantially reduce training time and parameter count for fine-tuning large models. It may influence how practitioners design parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies across instruction following, mathematical reasoning, coding, and multi-turn conversation tasks. Among FFN down-projections alone, the single dominant module accounts for 74.7–79.0% of the aggregate PAGE, and these proportions remain stable from Step 0 to Step 390. DomLoRA reduces training time by up to 2.74× compared with broad placement, though the dominant module's layer index is architecture-dependent but task-stable.

## [RoP Learns Path Rewards for Knowledge Graph Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10791) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Reward on Path (RoP), a framework that learns a lightweight, question-conditioned path reward from answer labels using an asymmetric objective. It then trains an LLM-based relation path generator via reward distillation and on-policy GRPO optimization, improving F1 by at least 2.6% over answer-derived methods on multiple KGQA datasets. This addresses a key bottleneck in KGQA: answer-derived supervision treats every answer-reaching path as correct, producing noisy training signals, while LLM-refined supervision is costly. RoP offers a cheaper alternative that outperforms LLM-refined methods without expensive supervision construction, which could benefit researchers in knowledge graph reasoning and LLM-based QA. The asymmetric objective supervises paths reaching the same answer jointly as a bag to learn their relative contributions, while penalizing each path individually for retrieving non-answer entities. The generator is trained in two stages: reward distillation transfers reward-induced preferences over candidate paths, and on-policy GRPO refines the policy on self-generated paths, with generated paths grounded in the KG to retrieve evidence.

Ego2World is a new executable benchmark that compiles egocentric cooking videos from the HD-EPIC dataset into symbolic worlds governed by graph-transition rules, allowing embodied agents to be evaluated on planning under partial observability. During evaluation, the simulator maintains a hidden world graph while the agent plans over its own partial belief graph using only local observations and execution feedback. This benchmark addresses a gap in embodied AI evaluation by bridging passive egocentric video datasets and synthetic interactive simulators, forcing agents to maintain belief memory and replan without observing the true world state. It suggests that belief maintenance should become a first-class target of embodied-agent evaluation, which could influence how future household robots and planning systems are tested. The benchmark derives reusable transition rules from video annotations and executes them in a hidden symbolic world graph, separating the simulator's true state from the agent's partial belief graph. Experiments show that action-overlap scores overestimate physical-state success, and that persistent belief memory improves task completion while reducing repeated visual exploration.

Researchers propose Palette, a modular framework that selectively relaxes refusal behavior for authorized target domains in LLMs while preserving standard safety elsewhere. It identifies a refusal direction via multi-objective search and internalizes it through lightweight adaptation, and supports modular composition of domain-specific safety controls via parameter merging without retraining. Current one-size-fits-all safety alignment causes models to refuse legitimate requests from authorized professionals, limiting helpfulness in specialized settings. Palette learns domain-specific safety controls independently and composes them through parameter merging, enabling on-demand multi-domain authorization without retraining. Experiments across four safety benchmarks, multiple model variants, and both LLMs and VLMs show precise safety control without sacrificing general utility.

Researchers introduced OSGuard, a dual-granularity benchmark suite for evaluating safety in computer-use agents, combining an action-level benchmark of 324 human-annotated examples with a risk-augmented execution suite of 45 tasks derived from 40 OSWorld tasks. The strongest evaluated guardrail reached 79.9% accuracy and 0.80 macro-F1 on the action-level benchmark, but performance dropped substantially on actions from risk-augmented executions, and adding the strongest guardrail only reduced unsafe task completion from 37.8% to 33.3%. As computer-use agents increasingly operate real desktops and applications, ensuring they respect state-dependent safety constraints becomes critical for deployment in sensitive environments. OSGuard provides a concrete, reproducible tool for measuring and improving agent safety, filling a gap between abstract safety research and practical guardrail evaluation. The action-level benchmark labels candidate actions as allowed, unrelated, or unsafe given the original instruction and current interface state, while the risk-augmented suite keeps original instructions unchanged but modifies the environment to introduce state-dependent safety constraints and preserve a safe completion path. Augmented evaluators retain original task-success criteria and add explicit state-based safety checks, distinguishing safe completion from nominal success that violates constraints.

## [Calibration Is Not Control: Intervention Utility for LLM-Agent Oversight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21399) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.21399v2) argues that runtime oversight of LLM agents should trigger interventions based on intervention utility rather than calibrated failure scores, formalizing when a summary is sufficient for intervention decisions and the utility lost when it is not. On ALFWorld, holding features, estimator, and router fixed while switching the supervision target from failure to intervention utility cut regret from 0.51 to 0.09, a gain that replicated on a second suite of mid-episode prefixes. The result suggests that widely used failure-risk thresholds may be the wrong control signal for agent oversight, since states with identical failure risk can differ in whether intervening actually helps. This reframes how safety and reliability teams should evaluate oversight signals — by the decisions they support, not just their predictive quality — and could change how handoff and escalation policies are designed for deployed agents. The authors evaluate by replaying agent prefixes and executing alternative actions from the same state; online, on 300 unseen tasks with a fixed stronger-model handoff, a frozen prefix-feature controller improved utility over failure-triggered routing, handing off less often (35% vs 48%) and succeeding more often (45% vs 37%). The gains depend on intervention value and are small on two reasoning benchmarks, and code is available at the project's GitHub repository.

## [Critic Experience Bank Enables Training-Free Step-Level Confidence for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12397) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Critic Experience Bank (CEB), a training-free framework that converts feedback from completed agent trajectories into reusable evidence for step-level confidence estimation. After each trajectory, an LLM assigns hindsight productivity pseudo-labels to individual actions and stores them alongside the critic's pre-execution confidence, task context, action, and observed feedback, allowing a fixed LLM critic to adapt over a task stream without parameter updates or ground-truth step labels. Reliable deployment of LLM agents in stateful environments requires knowing before execution whether an action will advance the task, since a single erroneous step can waste limited interaction budget or cause irreversible effects. CEB achieves the best or tied-best ECE, Brier score, and AUC in all twelve benchmark-backbone settings, reducing ECE by up to 53.8% relative to the strongest training-free baseline, which could influence future work on reliable and safe LLM agents. CEB is evaluated across four agent benchmarks spanning offline and live web navigation, mobile GUI and shell tasks, and three critic backbones, using rule-based step labels. Its confidence scores also improve downstream utility in selective execution and simulated task success, though the approach relies on hindsight pseudo-labels rather than ground-truth step labels at deployment.
