## [MARS: Multi-resolution Adaptive Routing for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07505) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07505) introduces MARS, a multi-resolution user memory that writes full user history into recurrent state tracks with different half-lives, paired with a sparse routing reader that selects relevant temporal resolutions per seed. It identifies a failure mode called 'temporal aliasing' and outperforms strong baselines on three public datasets, with gains growing as history length increases. Long-history sequential recommendation is central to modern recommender systems, and MARS shows that monolithic cached memories preserve temporal scales unevenly, a problem that worsens with longer histories. By addressing temporal aliasing with multi-resolution memory and sparse routing, it offers a practical path to better personalization at scale without sacrificing serving efficiency. MARS maintains fixed-size candidate scoring and achieves about 1.02x the warm-cache serving latency of its interface-matched baseline for 1,000 candidates per user. Ablations with paired tests confirm that temporal diversity and selective routing each contribute beyond hard-window memories or added capacity, and the advantage widens after within-user behavioral shifts.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Sequential recommendation models predict the next item a user will interact with based on their ordered history. Many long-history systems compress each user's history into a compact, candidate-independent memory that is cached and reused to score large candidate pools efficiently. Temporal aliasing refers to the uneven preservation of short-, medium-, and long-term signals in such monolithic memories, analogous to signal aliasing in signal processing. Sparse routing, inspired by mixture-of-experts, dynamically selects specialized sub-networks or memory tracks for each input.

SPL is a training-time augmentation rather than a new algorithm, and it is evaluated across multiple policy-based MARL backbones, environments, and staggered-participation patterns, including 60 MPE/RWARE comparisons and a physics-based UAV-UGV environment in Isaac Lab. ## [LOGIC: A New LLM Benchmark for Aerospace Change Impact Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07580) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced LOGIC, a controlled benchmark and evaluation framework that uses locally deployable language models to ground engineering change requests in aerospace electrical systems before propagating selected changes through a typed electrical traceability graph. The benchmark contains 168 scenarios (144 selection and 24 abstention cases) and evaluates three 7-8B models against intent-agnostic, lexical, and structured-evidence methods, separating candidate-selection errors from downstream propagation errors. This work addresses a specific but safety-critical problem: engineering change requests in aerospace often authorize only a subset of detected design differences, so propagating every difference can produce overly broad and potentially unsafe impact reports. By separating intent grounding from propagation, LOGIC offers a way to measure where LLM-based change-impact tools fail, which matters for engineers adopting AI assistance in regulated electrical design workflows. On 96 explicitly anchored selection cases, gate-only structured evidence achieved candidate F1 of 1.0000 versus 0.9677 for token-lexical matching, but on 12 relational-paraphrase cases token-lexical F1 was 0.1772 and gate-only F1 was 0.0000, while the LLMs reached 0.5000-0.6400. Model grounding degraded as candidate inventories grew from 4 to 64 changes, and an exploratory evidence-empty abstention policy raised strict abstention accuracy to 0.6667 and reduced unsafe-report rates to 0.1667, at the cost of 16.0-27.1 percentage points of answerable-case coverage.

## [LSC-DPO dynamically regulates DPO's sigmoid learning signal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07592) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07592) proposes Learning-Signal-Controlled Direct Preference Optimization (LSC-DPO), which reframes DPO from a loss-level geometric perspective and identifies the sigmoid factor as a learning signal that governs the objective's local sensitivity. LSC-DPO dynamically regulates this signal near a target regime, with a log-space analysis establishing conditions for stable tracking, and reports consistent improvements over DPO and strong preference-optimization baselines on AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH. DPO is a widely used reward-model-free alignment method, and its logistic loss becomes progressively less sensitive as the scaled preference margin grows during training, which can slow or stall learning. By explicitly controlling this sensitivity, LSC-DPO offers a lightweight, loss-level fix that could improve alignment quality for practitioners fine-tuning LLMs without adding a reward model. The method's log-space analysis derives conditions for stable tracking of the target learning-signal regime, and the authors observe that different coefficient initializations produce distinct transient learning-signal trajectories even when later signal levels converge. Based on this, they derive a signal-budget compensation rule that adjusts the target learning signal to offset these transient differences, substantially reducing performance variation across coefficient initializations.

**Background**: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a reward-model-free approach introduced in 2023 for aligning language models with human preference data, avoiding the need to sample from the language model during fine-tuning or to tune a separate reward model. It optimizes a logistic-style loss over pairs of preferred and rejected responses, where the sigmoid factor controls how strongly the loss reacts to changes in the preference margin. AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Anthropic-HH are standard benchmarks for instruction following and multi-turn dialogue alignment used to compare such methods.

## [SUTURE: Structured Verification from Rollout Groups for Video Temporal Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07601) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces SUTURE, a verifier for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that conditions scoring on the entire rollout group rather than scoring each rollout independently. It exploits disagreement across rollouts to reweight the target and coverage at each position to redistribute reward mass, and proves the verifier decomposes exactly into a standard IoU term plus a covariance correction determined by the rollout group. This work shows that the joint structure of a rollout group can yield a more informative reward signal for video temporal grounding, improving performance across five benchmarks and every reported IoU threshold. It also reduces video-start anchoring in reasoning traces, suggesting structured verification could improve both accuracy and interpretability in RLVR pipelines for vision-language tasks. A local gradient diagnostic reveals a preference for responses covering relatively less supported target regions in the analyzed groups, and the trained policy shows less video-start anchoring: for later events, the first temporal mention more often overlaps the annotated target. The approach is evaluated on five temporal grounding benchmarks, though the abstract does not specify model scale or computational overhead.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Video temporal grounding is the task of localizing the start and end timestamps of a video segment that matches a natural language query in an untrimmed video. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) adapts pretrained models by giving rewards based on objectively checkable outcomes, and in this setting generated temporal intervals can be scored directly against ground-truth intervals using overlap measures such as IoU. Existing overlap verifiers typically score each rollout independently, ignoring the joint structure of the rollout group.

The authors show that LFHE's structural score has an exact interpretation via graph Dirichlet energy — its sum across clients equals twice the representation Dirichlet energy — and report competitive performance across four image, speech, and text benchmarks. Matched-protocol controls identify the structural term as the principal empirical topology-selection signal, and comparison with broader peer discovery exposes a trade-off between predictive performance and discovery-state locality.

It also connects logic teaching to broader trends in automated reasoning, normative reasoning, and ethical/legal AI, where the same LogiKEy embeddings are used for research-grade modeling. The methodology relies on semantical embeddings in expressive classical HOL, so a single environment like Isabelle/HOL—together with its automated theorem provers and (counter-)model finders—can host propositional, modal, dynamic epistemic, deontic, dyadic deontic, and higher-order metaphysical logics. A new arXiv paper (2610.08231) introduces OSFP4 (Optimized Smoothing and Scaling for NVFP4), a quantization scheme that jointly optimizes a per-linear-projection diagonal smoothing matrix and block scales to minimize squared matrix-product quantization error under NVFP4. The method accounts for the rounding procedure (round-to-nearest or GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation) and is enabled by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one. NVFP4 is a 4-bit floating-point format for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs that reduces memory bandwidth and storage for LLM inference while aiming to keep accuracy close to higher-precision formats, so improving its accuracy without sacrificing throughput matters for practitioners deploying large models. OSFP4 reports the highest average accuracy among evaluated competitors in the corresponding quantization settings while retaining approximately 94-97% of vendor NVFP4 prefill throughput on measured workloads. The joint optimization is facilitated by analyzing a multiplicative-dither FP4 quantizer instead of the fixed deterministic one, and the scheme supports both round-to-nearest and GPTQ-style successive interference cancellation rounding. The internally prespecified contrast by prefix placement is a wide null, and the naive "has-written" label actually measures trajectory phase rather than harm. The best trigger beats the random-rule expectation on count but not on burden mass (a post hoc comparison), and whether it beats a token-budget rule at matched retention cannot be evaluated on the current release.

## [DART-ES Improves Backprop-Free LLM Fine-Tuning via Difficulty-Aware Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06993) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.06993) introduces DART-ES, which augments Evolution Strategies-based LLM fine-tuning with difficulty-aware reweighting and targeted replay of rare solvable samples. It outperforms standard ES on all five base models, raising average accuracy from 72.07% to 73.53% on GSM8K, exceeding GRPO's 73.26%, and achieves 49.20% average accuracy across five math reasoning benchmarks versus 48.34% for ES. This work strengthens the case for Evolution Strategies as a memory-efficient, backpropagation-free alternative to reinforcement learning for post-training LLMs, an area that has recently gained traction as a scalable fine-tuning paradigm. The reported runtime and memory advantages over GRPO and even GRPO+LoRA could make full-parameter fine-tuning more accessible on limited hardware. DART-ES estimates each problem's local solvability from its pass rate across the perturbation population and aggregates historical observations into a dynamic difficulty state that guides both reweighting and replay, without adding a difficulty model or backpropagation. It reduces runtime per step by 15.2%–50.2% and peak memory per GPU by 21.1%–51.1% compared with GRPO, and shows gains in instruction tuning, code generation, and the Countdown task with a 14B model.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Evolution Strategies (ES) is a gradient-free optimization approach that fine-tunes LLMs using only forward computation, avoiding the memory cost of backpropagation. Standard ES uniformly averages rewards across problems and compresses population feedback into a single scalar, which limits its ability to reflect how each problem's learning value changes as the model improves. Difficulty-aware reweighting and replay are techniques that adjust training emphasis based on problem difficulty and revisit valuable samples, and this paper combines them with ES.

## [Anchor and Adapt: Asymmetric Prompt Learning for Few-Shot Industrial Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07016) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Anchor and Adapt, a two-stage prompt learning framework that first learns transferable normal and abnormal anchors from annotated auxiliary data, then freezes those anchors and adapts an additional normal branch using only a few target normal samples. Cross-dataset experiments between MVTec-AD and VisA under 1-, 2-, and 4-shot settings show competitive detection and localization performance without requiring synthetic anomaly generation. Few-shot industrial anomaly detection is bottlenecked by the fact that a handful of normal target images contain no direct defect supervision, so anomaly prompts are hard to learn and manual defect descriptions are costly. By decoupling anomaly semantics acquisition from target appearance adaptation, this work reduces dependence on category-specific anomaly templates and could make vision-language-based inspection more practical for new product lines with minimal data. The framework keeps the learned anchors fixed while adapting a separate normal branch, and uses text-anchor regularization to encourage consistency with a generic normal prior and separation from abnormal anchors. Controlled ablations assess the contributions of transferred anchors, asymmetric adaptation, dual-normal representations, and anchor regularization, though the approach still relies on annotated auxiliary data for Stage I.

Vision-language models such as CLIP can be adapted with learnable prompts, yet in one-class anomaly detection there are no defect samples to guide anomaly prompts, and prior methods either rely on manually specified defect descriptions or synthetic anomaly generation. Anchor and Adapt addresses this by learning anomaly semantics from auxiliary annotated data and then adapting only the normal side to the target samples.

## [Cross-Generation Advantage Measures Distributed Progress in Recursive Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07105) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07105) introduces cross-generation advantage (CGA), a marginally matched contrast between cross-generation and within-generation model pairs, to quantify what the authors call 'distributed progress' in recommendation recursive self-improvement (Rec-RSI). Across four datasets and three sequential encoders, the preferred retention regime varies by architecture: cross-generation pairing benefits GRU4Rec and SASRec, while FMLP initially favors within-generation pairing and shifts toward cross-generation pairing after a second update. The work reframes Rec-RSI evaluation: instead of assuming each round's latest model consolidates all progress, it shows that useful ranking decisions can reside in relations between generations, which could change how self-improving recommenders are trained and selected. A label-free rank-separation statistic predicts the stronger retention family in 12/12 first-update and 5/6 second-update settings, and the selected family beats the direct successor in 34/36 held-out trajectories. The rank-separation statistic is label-free at selection time, making it practical for deployment, but five transfer mechanisms do not consistently reproduce the gains in a single model, suggesting the effect is architecture-dependent. Code is available at https://github.com/Jinfeng-Xu/RecRSI.

Sequential recommendation models such as GRU4Rec (a GRU-based session model), SASRec (a self-attention Transformer model), and FMLP (a simpler MLP-based model) predict the next item from a user's behavior sequence. ## [AURORA Embeds Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion into Graph Summarization for Preference Aggregation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07128) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.07128) proposes AURORA, an EDI-constrained graph summarization method that models user preferences as a weighted attributed bipartite graph and uses a greedy coarsening algorithm to merge user nodes while enforcing three structural criteria: an equity gap constraint (ΔE), an intra-list diversity constraint (ILD), and a group inclusion constraint. Evaluated on five datasets across four domains — MovieLens 100k and 1M, libimseti.cz, Rate My Professors, and OpenAlex (2018–2023) — AURORA achieves the largest and most consistent diversity gains over classical voting rules such as Borda and Condorcet. Classical aggregation rules like Borda and Condorcet have no built-in mechanism to prevent results from systematically favoring majority groups, collapsing onto homogeneous items, or under-representing minorities, so embedding EDI preservation directly into the aggregation structure offers a more robust fairness–diversity trade-off than post-hoc correction. This matters for recommender systems and any platform that aggregates group preferences, since it could shape how collective outcomes are produced rather than merely patched afterward. On MovieLens 100k at k = 20, AURORA simultaneously improves all three EDI criteria over both Borda and Condorcet; on Rate My Professors it combines high diversity (ILD = 0.808) with the highest female item representation (60%) at a moderate equity cost, and it achieves the lowest equity gap (ΔE = 0.031) on OpenAlex, where Borda-based methods recommend zero female authors. However, on libimseti.cz — the only dataset where the sensitive attribute appears on both sides of the bipartite graph — the method does not reduce the equity gap, a limitation the authors connect to prior findings that demographic parity is not always an appropriate target.

**Background**: Graph summarization is a family of algorithms that condense large graphs into more compact representations while preserving key structural properties. Borda count and Condorcet method are classical voting rules for aggregating ranked preferences into a collective ranking, but they offer no inherent fairness guarantees. Intra-list diversity (ILD) is a common recommender-system metric that measures the variety of items within a single recommendation list, and equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) refers to the goal of ensuring fair representation across demographic groups in algorithmic outcomes.

## [Open CLM Judge Performs Near Chance on Public Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07177) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper evaluates Contrastive-LM's CLM-v0.1-8B as an LLM judge on five public preference benchmarks and one hallucination benchmark, finding it statistically indistinguishable from coin flipping on RM-Bench and JudgeBench and answering every HaluEval item with a constant label. The study also shows that while the model's raw confidences are overconfident by up to +0.401, a single pooled temperature fit on held-out calibration items reduces expected calibration error to at most 0.062. This is a rigorous negative result for the LLM-as-a-judge literature, showing that a contrastive decision model with the same parameter count as much stronger reward models and generative judges fails on hard evaluation tasks. It also demonstrates that calibrated confidence about a near-chance judge has almost no value for confidence-gated cascades, since 92.3% to 100% of items must be escalated to a strong judge at the preregistered 0.97 retention bar. CLM-v0.1-8B scores between 0.351 (best-of-four, chance 0.250) and 0.593 (pairwise, chance 0.500), while a reward model reaches 0.764 to 0.976 and a generative judge 0.611 to 0.778, with every gap significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. The model does show two useful properties: a decision order-flip rate of 0.0002 versus 0.2188 for the generative judge, and a length-preference shift of -0.023 versus -0.217.

## [LiRA Learns How to Split Shared Constraint Penalties Across Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07491) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Lagrangian Responsibility Allocation (LiRA), a method that learns each agent's share of a common Lagrange multiplier by optimizing social welfare over a finite training horizon. Across CityLearn, MABIM, Harvest, and MetaDrive, spanning 3 to 400 agents, LiRA improves average social welfare by up to 29% over uniform and agent-specific multiplier baselines. When multiple agents share a cost budget, a single common multiplier can enforce the aggregate constraint but says nothing about who should bear the penalty, and uniform penalties ignore how differently agents value their rewards. LiRA offers a principled, welfare-optimizing way to distribute that burden, which could improve fairness and efficiency in real-world multi-agent systems such as power grid control, traffic coordination, and shared-resource management. The multiplier enforces the aggregate budget while responsibility shares redistribute its influence without modifying the original rewards or constraints; for convex games under standard regularity conditions, varying these shares induces a smooth family of normalized generalized Nash equilibria. To optimize responsibility before convergence, the authors derive a welfare gradient that accounts for both learning updates and the induced change in data distribution, and they report that grid and driving costs stay within budget, inventory violations decrease, and Harvest uses its available budget more effectively.

**Background**: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies multiple learning agents that coexist in a shared environment, each pursuing its own reward, and it is closely tied to game theory and repeated games. Constrained optimization with Lagrangian methods handles problems where a solution must satisfy limits, using a Lagrange multiplier to fold constraints into the objective. A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where no player can gain by unilaterally changing strategy, and a generalized Nash equilibrium extends this to settings where players' feasible strategies depend on each other, as happens when agents share a common budget.

## [Shannon Information Preservation Does Not Guarantee Predictive Contribution Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07565) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.07565) formalizes Complementary Feature Domains (CFD) theory, proving that an invertible representation transformation can leave Shannon information about the target unchanged while still altering predictive contribution under a restricted decision family. The authors introduce a CFD contribution defect that quantifies how contextual contributions change under controlled recoding, and validate the mechanism with a controlled ECG experiment. This result challenges the common assumption in machine learning that preserving information is sufficient for preserving predictive value, which has implications for representation learning, feature selection, and multi-representation prediction systems. It suggests that evaluating representations purely by information-theoretic criteria may miss realization-dependent contributions that matter for downstream accuracy. For bounded Lipschitz utility, the paper shows that each coalition utility shift is bounded by the behavioral distance between the attainable action sets before and after recoding, and every contextual contribution defect is bounded by the sum of corresponding coalition incompatibilities. Exact behavioral closure yields invariance, while increasingly accurate compensation yields restoration; the ECG experiment confirms that a nonlinear bijective recoding preserves information in a frozen time-frequency representation but changes accuracy under a fixed affine learner, with the exact inverse restoring all tested coalition accuracies.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Shannon information measures how much a representation tells us about a target variable, and it is often assumed that if two representations carry the same Shannon information, they should be equally useful for prediction. Complementary Feature Domains (CFD) theory instead characterizes predictive value as a context-indexed contribution system jointly induced by representations and their realization family, meaning that how a representation is realized (e.g., through a specific learner or action set) affects its predictive contribution. Invertible transformations are mappings that can be reversed without losing information, and they are central to this work because they preserve Shannon information by construction.

## [WASD: Wasserstein-based Knowledge Distillation for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07706) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A KAIST research team (AAILab) proposed WASD, a knowledge distillation method for LLMs that uses a Wasserstein-based distance with a cost matrix derived from token embeddings to align teacher and student distributions. To keep computation tractable, they adopt the Sinkhorn divergence and derive a gradient-equivalent objective that avoids extra networks, with experiments showing consistent gains on instruction following, math reasoning, and code generation. Most existing LLM distillation methods compare teacher and student only through per-vocabulary probability values, ignoring the semantic relationships between tokens. By explicitly encoding token-space semantics into the alignment objective, WASD offers a practical way to make smaller, cheaper student models inherit more of a large teacher's capability, which matters for cost-sensitive deployment of LLMs. The method builds a cost matrix from token embeddings and uses the Sinkhorn divergence (an entropic-regularized optimal transport cost) to keep the Wasserstein computation tractable, deriving a gradient-equivalent objective that needs no additional networks. The implementation is publicly released at https://github.com/aailab-kaist/WASD, and the paper reports gains across multiple LLM families and scales.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model, typically by aligning their output probability distributions. Wasserstein distance, also known as the earth mover's distance, measures the minimum cost of transforming one probability distribution into another on a given metric space, and unlike KL divergence it is a true metric that accounts for the geometry of the underlying space. Sinkhorn divergence is a debiased, entropy-regularized version of optimal transport cost that makes such computations efficient and numerically stable.

A new arXiv paper introduces SufficientPlan, a deployment framework that reduces search and computation in world-model planning without modifying pretrained models or planner updates. It combines Paired Sequential Budget Certification (PSBC), which certifies a smaller model-task-specific planning budget within a predefined Full-performance tolerance, and Static-Context Reuse (SCR), which caches observation and goal representations across search iterations. World models enable goal-directed control through decision-time action search, but their deployment is often limited by conservatively large planning budgets that waste compute and increase latency. By showing that competitive task performance does not require agreement with the Full-budget action and that sufficient budgets vary across model-task pairs, SufficientPlan offers a practical way to make model-based planning more efficient for real-world deployment. The framework requires no modification to pretrained world models or planner updates, and experiments across multiple world-model backbones and visual-control tasks show substantial reductions in search budgets and planning latency while maintaining competitive control performance. PSBC uses paired closed-loop evidence to search for and certify a reduced budget within a predefined Full-performance tolerance, while SCR preserves candidate-dependent planning and selected actions.

## [QuAR: Single-Pass Test-Time Adaptation for Quantized Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08358) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Quantizer-Aligned Recalibration (QuAR), a single-pass test-time adaptation method for quantized vision transformers that requires no backpropagation and no parameter updates. On ImageNet-C with ViT-B, QuAR achieves the highest mean accuracy among state-of-the-art backprop-free TTA methods across 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-bit precision, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.28 points at 8 bits and 4.00 points at 3 bits, with 46% lower latency and only 0.17 MB of memory overhead. Quantized models are essential for deploying vision transformers on edge devices, but they degrade sharply under distribution shift, and existing TTA methods are often too costly or misaligned with quantized inference. QuAR offers a lightweight, backprop-free solution that could make quantized ViTs more robust in real-world edge deployments without sacrificing efficiency. QuAR works by recalibrating activations at the input to a frozen quantizer, mapping the test stream's running per-channel statistics back toward the source calibration, thereby reducing per-channel mismatch and restoring the code distribution. A single fixed configuration remains effective across continual streams, non-i.i.d. label shift, seven out-of-distribution suites, and three other backbones.

Explainable AI methods increasingly output multiple plausible explanations rather than a single one, so deciding which explanation to present becomes a real design problem with downstream consequences for trust and decision-making. ## [Finite-Sample Prediction Limits for Soft State Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32652) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper derives a finite-sample lower confidence bound on the smallest population root-mean-square prediction error achievable by any linear predictor with a bounded spectral norm, for a fixed soft state representation. It also establishes a Koopman and reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space adjoint interpretation under exact deterministic linear evolution, and validates the bound on a four-state system across 117,000 replicate datasets plus a Van der Pol representation on 32 independent datasets. This work provides a principled, data-driven way to certify whether a chosen soft state representation can support accurate linear prediction, without fitting a prediction matrix. It matters for machine learning and dynamical systems practitioners who need reliability guarantees before deploying linear models on learned representations. The bound is computed from independent evaluation pairs and compares variation in successor coordinates within each reference class against the improvement soft inputs could provide; a bound above a tolerance rules out that tolerance for the entire matrix class, while a zero bound is inconclusive. For Kernel Affine Hull Machine coordinates, reconstruction-score margins control disagreement with reference labels and enter the prediction-error bounds, and the reported bounds are positive at the fitted matrix norm but can become zero at larger norm limits.

The Koopman operator is a linear operator that describes the evolution of observables of a nonlinear dynamical system, enabling linear analysis of nonlinear dynamics. Kernel Affine Hull Machines (KAHMs) are geometrically inspired kernel methods that compute distances from a bounded geometric body in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space, and have been used for compute-efficient and differentially private learning.

A new arXiv paper (2604.13385v3) proposes a bi-objective evolutionary algorithm with a diversity-based change response mechanism for dynamic chance-constrained open-pit mine scheduling, where block economic values are stochastic and mining/processing capacities vary over time. The mechanism repairs a subset of infeasible solutions and injects additional feasible solutions upon detecting environmental changes, and experiments on six mining instances show it consistently outperforms a baseline re-evaluation strategy across four multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. This work is notable because it jointly addresses uncertainty and dynamic change, which are usually studied in isolation in real-world scheduling, and it offers a general change-response mechanism that could be transferred to other dynamic stochastic optimization problems in mining, energy, and logistics. It may benefit researchers in evolutionary computation and mining engineers seeking more robust long-term mine plans under volatile commodity prices and shifting operational capacities. The formulation is bi-objective, simultaneously maximizing expected discounted profit and minimizing its standard deviation, which gives decision-makers a risk-aware Pareto front rather than a single deterministic schedule. The evaluation covers six mining instances under different uncertainty levels and change frequencies, but the approach is validated only on synthetic or benchmark mining data and does not yet address real-time operational constraints or large-scale industrial deployment.

## [Stochastic Penalty-Barrier Method for Constrained Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18618) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces the Stochastic Penalty-Barrier Method (SPBM), which extends classical penalty and barrier methods with exponential dual averaging, a stabilized penalty schedule, and the Moreau envelope to handle non-smoothness. It analyzes mini-batch bias in the barrier function, proves the transformed problem's feasible set is contained in the original, and shows competitive results on fairness and physics-informed neural network benchmarks. Constrained machine learning is increasingly important for fairness-aware training and physics-informed neural networks, where models must satisfy domain-specific constraints. SPBM offers a theoretically grounded and computationally efficient alternative, with per-epoch runtime largely independent of the number of constraints and within 1.3x of regularized Adam, making it practical for large-scale constrained problems. The method uses exponential averaging of dual variables and a stabilized penalty schedule, with the Moreau envelope addressing non-smoothness. On fairness benchmarks with 90 to 9900 constraints, per-epoch runtime is largely independent of constraint count and within 1.3x of regularized Adam, though the paper notes bias introduced by mini-batching in the barrier function.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Constrained machine learning (CML) formulates training as an optimization problem with equality or inequality constraints, enabling fairness-aware training, physics-informed neural networks, and integration of symbolic domain knowledge. Classical penalty methods replace constraints with penalty terms in the objective, while barrier methods (interior penalty functions) keep iterates strictly feasible. The Moreau envelope is a smoothing technique that makes non-differentiable functions continuously differentiable, allowing first-order methods to be applied. Dual averaging is an optimization technique that accumulates gradients to stabilize updates.

## [Terminal Representation Offers Eigenvector-Free RL Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.31289) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the terminal representation (TR), a reinforcement learning representation that encodes reward-weighted trajectories in a lower-dimensional form and can be used directly for option discovery, reward shaping, transfer learning, and exploration without computing eigenvectors. The authors develop the theoretical foundations, prove convergence of two learning algorithms, demonstrate zero-shot compositionality, and show empirically that TR reduces computational overhead for learning, storage, and use. The TR bypasses eigendecomposition, which not only lowers computational cost but also removes the assumption of symmetric transition dynamics that limits successor and default representations. This could make representation-driven RL more practical for real-world domains with asymmetric dynamics and for large-scale problems where eigenvector computation is prohibitive. The paper proves that the TR is embedded in the top eigenvector of the default representation, meaning it captures the same underlying knowledge without eigendecomposition. It also provides convergence guarantees for two learning algorithms and establishes equivalences between alternative reward formulations, though empirical validation is limited to subsidiary applications.

The successor representation (SR) encodes states by the future trajectories they induce, decoupling information flow from reward, while the default representation (DR) weights those trajectories by reward to integrate credit assignment. Eigenvectors of SR and DR have been used for downstream tasks like option discovery and reward shaping, but eigendecomposition is computationally expensive and assumes symmetric transition dynamics.

## [Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy Framework Diagnoses Prompt Injection Classifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26423) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.26423v2) proposes the Latent Diagnostic Taxonomy, a framework that builds a dimensionality-optimized prompt injection classifier and then diagnoses which of its confident decisions can be trusted. Applied to a public prompt injection dataset, the framework finds that roughly 77% of the classifier's confident decisions are not robust to removing a single token, and that this brittleness splits into two distinct failure patterns: a confidence calibration failure and a genuinely exploitable shortcut. Prompt injection is a major security threat to LLM applications, and classifiers are commonly deployed as safeguard layers, so knowing which of their confident decisions can actually be trusted is critical for safe deployment. The framework's finding that most confident decisions are brittle to single-token removal suggests many existing prompt injection safeguards may be far less reliable than their confidence scores imply. The framework has three steps: empirically selecting embedding dimensionality via cross-validated performance rather than fixing it a priori; locating a small set of latent support vectors (~29% of training examples) that identify tokens altering the predicted label; and using those tokens and their attack magnitudes to build a diagnostic taxonomy. The taxonomy routes prompts into four zones — rely Safely, flag Heuristic Bias, flag Heuristic Override, and route Insufficient Context for human/safety review — with remediation strategies recommended for each.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 7, 04:00

**Background**: Prompt injection is a cybersecurity exploit in which carefully crafted inputs cause a machine learning model, especially a large language model, to behave in unintended ways, bypassing safeguards because the model cannot reliably distinguish developer instructions from user input. Many defenses add a separate classifier as a safeguard layer that flags malicious prompts, but such classifiers can be fooled by small input perturbations. Support vector machines are classic classifiers that base decisions on a subset of influential training examples called support vectors, and this paper extends that idea to latent support vectors in embedding space to diagnose classifier behavior.
